speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PORT BORDEN-CAPE TORMENTINE    REQUEST FOR IMPROVED FERRY SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Minister of Transport. I should like to ask the minister what steps his department is taking toward providing an additional ferry for service between Borden, Prince Edward Island and Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PORT BORDEN-CAPE TORMENTINE    REQUEST FOR IMPROVED FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Queens for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question.
The Department of Transport has carefully reviewed the need for additional ferry service between Borden and Cape Tormentine. The advisability of purchasing the Vacationland for this service was carefully considered, and I wish to advise that in the opinion of the department the ship, as is, would not be suitable. To make the Vacationland suitable for the service involved would require changing the form of the ship, adding accommodation, a complete conversion of machinery and fitting the vessel with firefighting and other equipment required for this class of ship in Canada. These necessary alterations it is estimated would cost approximately $2 million, and the ship could not be ready for use until well into 1960.
It is proposed to undertake as early as possible the construction of a new ferry for this service, with a view to placing a ship in service some time in 1961. The ship proposed would be adequate to meet the increasing demand for automobile transportation and would be suitable for service elsewhere should the construction of a causeway to Prince Edward Island result in this vessel not being required between Borden and Tormentine.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the final accounting of the 1957-58 wheat pool which was closed out on May 15 has been completed. An interim payment was made in March in respect of this pool amounting to over $38 million. The basis of the interim payment was 10 cents per bushel on all grades of wheat excepting high quality milling grades of Durum wheat upon which the interim payment was 15 cents per bushel.
The final payment will amount to over $33 million-$33,874,398.61, to be exact-after providing for payment costs and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act levy. The average final payment will, therefore, amount to just under 9 cents a bushel-8.98856 cents per bushel in exact figures. Total prices realized by producers for the principal grades of wheat delivered to the 1957-58 pool are higher than the total prices received for the preceding crop year. The Canadian wheat board has advised me that it is in a position to commence issuing final payment cheques to producers immediately.
Since the final payment is somewhat less than the estimate made by the farm organizations in asking for deficiency payments, will the government now give serious consideration to their request?

I would point out that the final payment is higher this year than it was last year. It is higher by 4 cents on No. 1 northern, by 4 cents on No. 2 northern, by 2 cents on No. 3 northern and by 2 cents on No. 4 northern, increases which show that this year was a much better one than last year.

AH orders in council made under this section while parliament is in session shall be laid before parliament during such session and, if made while parliament is not in session, shaU be laid before parliament at the next ensuing session.

As a matter of fact, of late, the chambers of commerce on both sides of the river have given continued attention to this problem. At a sort of forum, sponsored by the French chamber of commerce of Ottawa, we have discussed that matter rather fully, replying to all questions that were put to us. As a result, the members came to the conclusion that someone should take the initiative, otherwise nothing concrete would be achieved. Besides, I remember that, in this regard, as early as 1955, Mr. Winters, predecessor of the present hon. minister, had earnestly attempted to get the provincial governments to participate in the construction of that bridge. We know that the Ontario government did not make any formal pledge at that time, but in any case I note that, on October 29, 1955, Mr. Frost said:
(Text):
In connection with the proposed Ottawa-Hulll bridge, it is of course understood that this is merely for a preliminary meeting which in no way will commit any of the governments to this project.
Will you please contact Mr. Allan, to whom I am sending a copy of this letter?
(Translation) :
This was an indication that the Ontario government was at least ready to give serious consideration to the matter. Moreover, as a result of that letter, Mr. Allan made the following reply dated November 29, 1955:
(Text):
I have noted your invitation to appoint an engineer to serve on a committee in connection with the proposed bridge, and am pleased to recommend Mr. J. B. Wilkes, district engineer in Ottawa, as a member of the proposed committee.
(Translation):
This shows that, as early as 1955, the Ontario government had intended to give the matter serious consideration. On the other hand, I note that even in 1957, the Quebec government ignored the matter entirely. In fact, I have here a copy of a letter written by Mr. Winters to the premier of the province of Quebec, in which he made the following statement:
I informed you on November 10, 1956 of our intent to set up a committee to go into the matter of rebuilding the approaches to the existing bridges between Ottawa and Hull, the possible location of a
Supply-Public Works new bridge, and a preliminary assessment of the costs involved. I invited you to send a representative to this committee.
The committee has prepared a report, and I enclose for your information a copy of the proceedings of its last meeting, held December 14, 1956, together with a copy of the report from the consulting engineer recommending construction of a new bridge.
I shall welcome any comment you may wish to submit concerning this proposal.
That letter went unanswered. Now apparently the only objection which remains at this time is the opposition of the Quebec premier who, in answer to a question, in the provincial legislature, said: "If Ottawa want bridges, let them build themselves some."
The matter, it seems to me, should be outside of politics. The situation is such that we cannot put up with it much longer. That is why I ask the minister if he could not intimate to his successor.-as the session is soon to be prorogued so that he will probably be replaced in this post-that the Minister of Public Works in Ottawa should be the very man to go ahead and continue the work already begun by his predecessor, Mr. Winters, so as to convince the provincial authorities both of Ontario and Quebec of the fact that in the national capital the position is becoming more intolerable every day.
I know that, if the minister were to consider this request, talks might be resumed and, with some good will on the part of provincial governments-in as much as the minister has already stated with regard to this matter that the federal government is still prepared to pay its share-and, as I said, with some good will and good grace on the part of provincial governments, we could in two or three years see at least the beginning of a solution to that problem, which is the dearest wish of the people of both cities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, would you allow me to take up another point. There are in the Ottawa area many government buildings, most of which, except perhaps the national printing bureau, are on the Ontario side of the river. Some of those buildings are quite a distance from parliament. In fact, some of them are as far as Manotick, several miles from downtown Ottawa.
In the Quebec part of the national capital area there are very few federal buildings. Yet the various governments have expressed the wish that an area of about 35 square miles on the Quebec side be included in the national capital plan.

I wonder why there are not more federal buildings located in the Quebec area, where they would be much closer to the parliament buildings. I am not, of course, referring to structures which are part of the experimental farm; it is only logical and reasonable that these should be out there, I am referring particularly to those buildings which accommodate the various divisions of the Public Works or the Post Office department, and have been erected still farther from the centre block. In the Quebec part of the national capital area there are very few such new buildings.
Mr. Chairman, I know that when in the committee of public accounts, the project of building the National Printing Bureau on the Quebec side was under discussion the first question asked by a member of that committee was: "Why should the National Printing Bureau be located in Hull?" Such attitude shows that some people are narrowminded to a degree that we, who are broadminded, are unable to understand. Some people seem to think that no public building can be erected on the Quebec side. Yet the ridings of Gatineau and Hull comprise space that would be most appropriate for new federal constructions. The federal government would thus be enabled to spread its bounties on both sides of the national capital.
Mr. Chairman, I have not brought up this problem for the purpose of criticizing the present Minister of Public Works. I know he has not had the time to consider all those matters in the short time he has been heading the department. I am pointing out the situation not because of anything that happened in the past, but rather to avoid problems that might arise in the future. Let the Quebec part of the national capital receive greater attention, and I am convinced that everyone will be happy.
Mr. Chairman, I had promised to be brief. In closing, I wish to repeat what I was just saying, that the Minister of Public Works, in view of his new appointment, will soon be stepping out of his present job, and will also be relinquishing his duties as house leader. However, before resuming my seat, may I be allowed to make a suggestion to the government? There is in this house a man whose knowledge of the standing orders and procedure of the house is truly remarkable, a man who reasons with perfect logic and who has been presiding over the pro-


ceedings of a particular committee with such fairmindedness that he should be the unanimous choice of the cabinet to succeed the hon. Minister of Public Works. I therefore suggest to the government that they consider appointing the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small) in that capacity, in view of all his outstanding qualifications.

Mr. Chairman, it is with pleasure that I associate myself with all members of the house in warmly congratulating the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) on his appointment to the important function of Secretary of State for External Affairs. That mark of confidence on the part of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the compliments showered upon him by members of all political parties represented here, prove that the minister has all the qualities required to fulfil this task.
If we rejoice upon his appointment, it is nonetheless true that we are a bit sorry to see him leave the Department of Public Works, which he has headed since 1957 and which he had administered with devotion, wisdom and in the interest of the whole country.
For my part, I know I have taken much of his time. The requests I have put to him have been many, and if they were more numerous than those of other members, it is because the beautiful constituency of Gaspe, which I have the honour to represent here in the house, is one which has been the most neglected in the past. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, those requests were not made for political reasons, but rather in the interest of a constituency which is rich thanks to its fisheries, its forests and its mines, but hardly developed from an economic standpoint, and that on account of a scarcity of means of communications, both by water and by land.
I have asked for a fishing harbour for Newport, and I may say that my request was considered with close attention by the minister, by his devoted deputy minister and by the whole staff of the department. The authorities came to the conclusion that my request was justified, and they granted it in favour of the city of Newport, and therefore of the constituency of Gaspe. Thanks to the subsidy which the department decided to grant for the construction of a convenient fishing harbour, I am proud to announce to the house that the Quebec United Fishermen will build a filleting plant at a cost of more than one million dollars and that plant will help improve the lot of fishermen, and at the same time, will provide jobs for more than 150 persons.

That is, Mr. Chairman, something which is practical for the development of my constituency. Attention was given not only to the interest of a small group, but to the whole community, including those poor fishermen.
I know I have put other requests to the minister, and, as I said a moment ago, they were numerous.
One of those dealt with improvements to be made to the harbour of Grande Riviere, which comprises a population of fishermen and a federal biology office as well as a provincial fisheries school. The Robin, Jones & Whitman Company of Paspebiac, would be interested in the building of a fish processing plant. That company is willing to invest $500,000 in such a plant. It is ready to start construction as soon as the Department of Public Works decides to undertake the work that is needed on the harbour. I am confident that the minister and his officials will act upon this request, so that the parish may have the benefit of a new important industry.
Mr. Chairman, I have also called for improvements to the Chandler harbour, which has been the subject of representations for many years. The Gaspesia sulphite plant is located in that city, and many ships call at this port to take on cargo. However, the ships have to put up with considerable difficulties, because at the slightest indication of a storm they have to get away from the wharf and keep out at sea for hours and even days, thus further increasing the cost of lumber transportation; this, in turn, prevents companies from paying as much for the wood as they pay in other communities with more adequate transportation facilities.
The city of Chandler has a magnificent port, where ships can dock at any time of the year. In the wintertime, there is no ice to obstruct traffic. I have here a photograph taken in February, which shows that there is no ice to prevent shipping, so that ships can come in and take up cargo throughout the year.
If you want to have an idea of that industry, which is vital both for the town of Chandler and the constituency of Gaspe in general, I must tell you that in 1950 the company spent for wood alone an amount of $2,352,000; in 1956, it spent $4,258,000. That same company has paid in wages in 1950, $1,461,000, and in 1956 $1,983,000. It adds up, for 1956, in purchases of wood and in wages, to $6,241,000. Besides that company intends to enlarge its plant, which would provide more work to the labourers.

In that case too, we are waiting, for I am sure the minister will do something to improve the situation. The officers of the Department of Public Works have undertaken a study of that project. A scale model has been prepared. I have had the opportunity to look at it with a delegation which had come from Chandler to meet the Minister of Public Works and his deputy. I am sure that this project will materialize in the near future. I realize that all the requests I have made cannot be answered overnight, especially when those made on behalf of my constituency are so numerous. I am confident that in the near future, the minister will give consideration to the development of that area, one which has been neglected in the past.
I would like to add a few words about Gaspe harbour, one of the most beautiful of natural harbours. Unfortunately, it has remained in its natural state, just as created by Providence. There again, it would be possible to do something, because we, in the Gaspe constituency, have, like everyone else, paid taxes; unfortunately, we have never got back part of that money for the improvement of the economic situation of the area. As I said last year, we cannot take advantage of all the good legislation adopted by the government, as do other constituencies; we get practically no benefit under the National Housing Act, that excellent piece of legislation.
In conclusion, I once more thank the minister and all his staff for the consideration they have given in the past to the problems of Gaspe.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very brief remark to make about paraplegics and public buildings, but before I do so may I second the remarks of the hon. member for York-Scarborough on behalf of the G.F.A. on the new honours which have come to the minister. We have watched his progress with a great deal of interest, and as he continues to rise in the affection of the house he nears the day when he too will become a member of the G.F.A.
My remarks regarding paraplegics are very simple. I have had representations from time to time, as I know other members of this committee have, in which the paraplegic associations have expressed some concern about

Supply-Public Works
the architecture of public buildings. Particularly they do wish that the federal government in its building program would give some lead, direction or example to the other groups building in this country by so arranging the entrances that it is possible for people in wheel chairs to enter and leave public buildings with the utmost of ease. I hope when the minister rises to take part in this debate he might deal specifically with the representations that have been made by the paraplegic associations.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to extend congratulations to the minister on his appointment to the external affairs post. He must, even with his usual modesty, feel a sense of pride on his selection to this most important post in international affairs. It becomes, I think, a recognition of 24 years of faithful service as a member of the parliament of Canada, and for the past two years as a federal cabinet minister in the important portfolio of public works; also he has fulfilled the difficult assignment of house leader. It is a deserved appointment for many reasons, not the least of which is his 24 years of faithful service as a member of parliament. Of course his many other attributes are good reasons for his selection. Every good wish goes to the minister in his role in international affairs. He will now serve Canada in a wider field, and I join with others and say to the minister good luck; good deliberations in the best interests of Canada.
The minister in his remarks on May 2, when opening the main public works estimates, stated that the total departmental expenditure for the year 1958-59 was $220.3 million, an increase of $8 million over the year 1957-58. This year's total amount requested, exclusive of statutory items, is $173.6 million, a decrease of $17.8 million compared to last year's amount. The supplementary estimates tabled on June 1 provide an additional $700,000 for New Brunswick under the heading "harbours and rivers, engineering services". Under the heading of public works for New Brunswick the amount shown for 1958-59 is $2,005,000, and the amount for 1959-60 is $490,000.
Under the heading of public buildings in the Atlantic provinces the 1958-59 total was $6,938,475 compared with the 1959-60 total of $4,248,475, a difference of $2,690,000. Under the heading dealing with public buildings in New Brunswick there are two votes for the completion of the construction of public buildings at Campbellton and Grand Falls and three votes for the construction of new
[Mr. McCleave.l
buildings at Moncton, Sackville and Saint John. Almost the whole decrease of $1,746,000 under public buildings for the three maritime provinces falls to the lot of New Brunswick namely $1,515,000 or 87 per cent of the total decrease.
Under the provision for harbours and rivers in New Brunswick in this year's estimates, Northumberland-Miramichi has only three small wharf repair jobs; Escuminac breakwater repairs at $59,000, Lower Newcastle wharf repairs at $26,500 and Newcastle wharf repairs at $70,000 for a total of $155,000, which is more than will be required since the low bids on these jobs are below the estimated costs.
There are many single items in the list of projects for other parts of New Brunswick which amount to many times the total amount to be spent in Northumberland-Miramichi, even though there are a number of small projects needed in that constituency. These include small landing wharfs, extensions to existing wharves and dredging to improve the Miramichi fishing industry. I trust that when the further supplementary estimates are brought down many of these projects will be included.
I ask the minister to grant the request recently made by the fishermen of Manuels post office and have the necessary survey undertaken immediately. I also request the minister to have his New Brunswick officials make a complete survey of Miramichi fishing facilities with a view to constructing new facilities where none presently exist, and improving existing ones to ameliorate the lot of the fishermen who, as primary producers, toil the hardest for the least return received by any segment of Canadian workers.
When the amendment to the Trans-Canada Highway Act was before the house earlier this session to increase the amount of the fund, I urged the minister to promote a second trans-Canada highway in the northeast section of New Brunswick. This secondary highway would provide a much-needed complete artery from Campbellton to Moncton, filling in the missing link in the highway transportation system in that area at Chatham, where a serious traffic bottleneck exists. Perhaps the minister would give consideration to presenting legislation next session which would make it possible for the federal and provincial governments to enter into agreements for the construction of vital secondary transportation arteries.
In connection with highways other than primary or secondary trans-Canada highways, the citizens of northern and eastern New Brunswick are aroused over reports

that a corridor road is to be constructed between central Canada and southern New Brunswick through the state of Maine. Reports state that federal assistance will be provided in conjunction with the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec. While it is realized that the federal government has no jurisdiction over any highway which the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec might construct, and that it certainly has no jurisdiction within the state of Maine, it is on any grounds inconceivable that the federal government would assist in any way in the construction of this proposed corridor road, a highway which would have an extremely adverse economic result in the northern and eastern sections of New Brunswick. The people in this area would appreciate the minister's views with regard to such federal assistance, and on their behalf I plead with the minister to use his influence to turn down any requests for aid.
A newspaper report which appeared in the Moncton Daily Times of May 9, 1959 stated that proposal of the provincial government to assist in the construction of a tourist wharf in the town had been accepted by the committee of the whole of the Shediac town council. The proposal was that the Shediac town council should provide $16,000, the provincial government $24,000 and the federal government the remaining $120,000.
Requests have been made by the Chatham town council for federal financial assistance toward the construction of a highway bridge, a project of much greater importance than the tourist wharf. Requests were also made to the provincial government in this connection, but both requests for assistance toward this bridge project fell on deaf ears. Apparently the ears are more receptive in the case of a tourist wharf. How can government assistance toward the construction of a tourist wharf be reconciled with refusal to grant assistance toward the building of a bridge on a main provincial highway? I am not objecting to assistance to the town of Shediac for a tourist wharf in this lobster capital of the world. I feel, however, that other undertakings are worthy of support, undertakings of a more vital nature which unfortunately have not been assisted.
On May 4 of this year, as reported in the Commercial-World, of May 7, 1959, representatives of the Chatham board of trade, R. J. Martin, M.L.A., J. W. Clarke and E. J. McKinnon, met with the Chatham town council and requested a grant of $1,000 in order to continue the campaign for a bridge at Chatham, $400 of this amount to be used to defray the expenses of a delegation to Ottawa to be undertaken-and here I quote
Supply-Public Works from the newspaper-"in an effort to get a commitment from public works Minister Green relative to the proposed bridge." The request for $400 to defray expenses to Ottawa was granted. The remainder was held in abeyance, with a decision to be made when the delegation had presented its report.
I do not know whether this delegation did visit Ottawa. If the delegation has in fact met the minister, then the citizens of Chatham and the surrounding area will appreciate learning from the hon. gentleman the results of the representation. The outcome of the meeting is awaited with great interest, and I hope when the minister sums up our discussions he will make reference to it. The May 6, 1958 issue of the Chatham Gazette reporting on a meeting of the bridge committee with the Minister of Public Works at Chatham a few days earlier stated:
At the conference held with Hon. Mr. Green every assurance was given the committee by Mr. Green that he would co-operate in every possible way and explore every available channel to enhance the erection of this bridge. It is therefore planned that the committee will, if necessary, journey to Ottawa and discuss the matter further with the hon. Minister of Public Works.

The May 6, 1958, issue of the Chatham Gazette. The same newspaper article also stated:
The bridge committee which met Hon. Howard Green, federal Minister of Public Works, here in Chatham, Is now seeking to arrange a conference with Hon. Hugh John Flemming, premier of New Brunswick, to explore prospects for immediate action for the survey and erection of this bridge.
Premier Flemming took no action toward a survey, the first essential step. However, the town council of Chatham authorized a survey which was completed recently at the town's expense. I do not know if the minister was misquoted in this newspaper article or if his remarks were received with too much optimism and were elaborated upon. Perhaps the reporter at the meeting was carried away with enthusiasm and misquoted the minister, because knowing the minister as I do I think he would be very careful in what he said about assistance in the erection of a bridge that forms part of a highway within a province.
On the other hand, if the minister was reported correctly then perhaps he will inform the committee what channels he explored to further the erection of the bridge. Perhaps he will tell the committee if he contacted the provincial authorities in this connection and, if so, with what results. Whatever action was taken by the minister, it is obvious that the federal government does not assume any responsibility.

On February 4, 1959, nine months less two days later, the minister was asked the following question by myself as recorded at page 674 of Hansard of that date:
Has the federal government any responsibility for New Brunswick highway No. 11-of which the proposed bridge at Chatham would form a part?
His reply on that occasion was as follows:
No responsibility in respect of New Brunswick highway No. 11. Should a bridge be constructed, however, there would be the normal approval required under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
This approval, known to most people, is to safeguard against obstructions to water navigation and does not provide for financial assistance. In view of the government's answer of February 4 of this year, it appears that nothing of a concrete nature can be gained by sending a delegation to Ottawa unless the provincial minister of public works were a member of the delegation and the plans of the provincial government were placed before the federal minister and were known to the members of the Chatham board of trade delegation.
This same newspaper article of May 6, 1958 promoted the view that it is essential that conferences be held with the provincial department of public works at Fredericton, seeking federal co-operation. Although conferences were held they brought no tangible results. It is my view that before any assistance can be secured at the federal level the provincial government must make its position clear; otherwise efforts will get the same runaround for this vitally needed bridge which is the treatment that has been received for some time.
On page 453 of the book of estimates there is an item of $360,000 to be voted for an investigation to determine the feasibility of constructing a proposed causeway across Northumberland strait, including the opening of a test quarry. The minister's statement in connection with the proposed Northumberland strait causeway was not very encouraging to the people of Prince Edward Island and many others. The minister outlined what was encountered in this survey with respect to tidal and ice conditions that will result if a causeway is constructed. He spoke of other factors that will be considered, following which the economic feasibility of the project will be decided.
If the minister is in a position to give an approximate date when a report will be issued or when an interim report will be made public, the people of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick would appreciate such an announcement. In any event they look for a report at the earliest possible date and urge that the matter be expedited. Now that 
the economic survey has been undertaken they are keenly conscious that the $184 million South Saskatchewan dam project is under way.
A disturbing incident took place recently that is detrimental to the building up of an efficient staff for the performance of a public service. Following the change in government in 1957 the employees of government dredges No. 23 and No. 24 were retained. Provincial officials in charge of the dredges expressed complete satisfaction with all these employees, who were trained men giving good service. Attempts were made in 1957 through political channels to have certain individuals fired. No changes were made in 1957 or in 1958, and crews were kept intact despite further political efforts.
One reason for the previous failure of political efforts to have certain members of the crews dismissed was that none of the crew members took any part whatever in the political campaigns of 1957 and 1958.
When operations commenced this season four of the crew were not called for work and to this day they have received no notice that they would be continued in employment. Four new men were taken on as replacements. These were men untrained in this type of work, with no previous experience on the water or with dredging equipment. In our experience with dredging equipment the dismissal of men who have served faithfully over the years is a retrograde step in the building up of the public service. The action was taken solely on political grounds, despite what the minister said with regard to employees of his department retaining their jobs as long as their services were satisfactory and they did not take part in politics.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question? Are these permanent employees about which the hon. member is speaking or temporary employees who are hired every year?
The minister well knows they were temporary employees hired each year, but regardless of that-

I might say that I know that in past years they were hired by the former government because they were political supporters of the Liberal party, and were hired on the recommendation of the hon. member who now has the floor.
Are you suggesting the same thing is happening now?

Regardless of that, Mr. Chairman, these men gave good service over the years and relinquished any political affiliations. I maintain they are deserving of

better treatment than they received, because of the excellent service they have faithfully rendered over the years.
Perhaps the minister tried to retain those experienced workers, as is indicated by the fact that no dismissals were made in 1957 or 1958, right until this year. However, it appears that the local political pressure became too strong, and the minister finally agreed to the termination of the service of trained personnel in favour of inexperienced men-and I trust the Minister of Veterans Affairs will listen to this-even displacing war veterans by non-veterans.
The minister's answer to the starred question evaded giving any good reason for the dismissals. The only answer given was that the jobs were seasonal positions, a very weak reason. In my opinion it was the machinery used to dismiss faithful and experienced employees who were branded as Liberals but who, despite what any local Conservative patronage committee may say, took no part in the 1957 or 1958 election campaigns. I trust the Minister of Veterans Affairs will note this, too. I probably realized at the start that the story-

I have noted a whole lot regarding the hon. member's constituency, and the main thing I have noticed in the past is this. In the years when his party was in power all the men who obtained employment were of his party and were recommended by him, and anyone belonging to any other party had no chance at all.

Well, that is the view of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and I know everybody realizes it is purely a political point of view on these matters. I am sure that in his long experience as a representative of the people when he was in the provincial government, and now that he holds the patronage here with the federal government, the minister never recommended any Liberal for any job under his jurisdiction.
You do not know that.

From the point of view of building up the public service and protecting the rights of employees gained through services rendered, and for the maintenance of a good level of production for public money expended in this essential service, it is unfortunate that this action was taken.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I repeat my request for a survey of fishing facilities directed toward new construction and improvements to existing facilities for the Mira-michi fishing industry. On behalf of the fishermen who are primary producers of many species of fish from Miramichi waters, who toil under great handicaps, who are deserving
Supply-Public Works of adequate facilities to assist them in their daily labours, I urge the minister, in co-operation with the Minister of Fisheries, to authorize a complete study and survey. At the same time a survey should be made of wharf and dredging facilities for the export and import trade of the Miramichi.

Mr. Chairman, I shall transgress only a short time on the committee's time to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his new appointment. It is perhaps the only opportunity that hon. members will have during this session to offer congratulations to the minister. I want him to bear in mind that this is not meant to contribute to a delay in the passage of his estimates.
Since he came to the cabinet almost two years ago the Minister of Public Works has done a very commendable job and a tremendous service to Canada, particularly to the Atlantic provinces. There are in the province of Newfoundland-indeed in the maritime provinces-many outstanding works which are evidences of the great interest of the Minister of Public Works in the less endowed areas of Canada.
I want to assure the minister of the high esteem in which he is held in my constituency in the province of Newfoundland. The interest he has taken in my province, as I say, has been made manifest on many occasions. My one regret is that because of time, because of the many demands on the minister, he has not had an opportunity since becoming Minister of Public Works to visit the province of Newfoundland and see for himself just exactly what a tremendous job is being undertaken by his department in that province.
I could speak, for example, of the mammoth St. John's harbour development, which in a few years' time will make this old seaport of St. John's into a great modern harbour. I think, too, of the community stage program, which has received a fair amount of criticism from some hon. members here and in other places as well. But I will say this with regard to that community stage program, Mr. Chairman. It is the first concrete and definite step that has been taken in many years by the federal government to materially aid the Newfoundland fishermen. It is my hope that this community stage program which is now in course of development stage-perhaps it could be termed an experimental stage-will be enlarged and extended in the years ahead.
Perhaps the greatest criticism that has been made of the community stage program is that it is inadequate in that it covers only 20 of the hard-pressed Newfoundland fishing centres; but we must realize that this is

Supply-Public Works something new, and it must proceed slowly on the basis of trial and error. I can only hope that as this community stage program proceeds it will meet with that degree of success which was intended.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Public Works has now been called upon to serve his country in the very important field of world diplomacy and world politics. I think it is a great tribute to his ability that he should be called upon to serve Canada in these troubled times. In paying this little tribute to the minister, as I said before, I do so with a certain amount of regret because he is leaving the portfolio of public works. To those who follow in his footsteps I suggest that he has set a standard which will be quite difficult to maintain. However, I am sure the minister will always retain that interest in Canadian affairs generally for which he has been noted down through the years.
Public works in a province such as Newfoundland play a more important role than in perhaps any other part of Canada, because they contribute not only to the material improvement of harbours, rivers and public buildings but also contribute greatly to the economy of this retarded area. One has just to scan the minister's estimates for this year to see that many important works are now being undertaken by the Department of Public Works which I suggest should have been started years ago. They have been started now because of that greater degree of interest which exists in the Department of Public Works.
I think of the huge wharf reconstruction at Bay de Verde; the wharf extension and shed at Bell island; the wharf reconstruction and extensions at Carmanville and Catalina; the harbour improvements at Codroy on the west coast; the huge wharf now under construction at Goose Bay, Labrador; the breakwater construction at Grand Bank; the building of the large wharf at Harbour Breton on the south coast; the wharf construction at Harbour Main; the harbour improvements at Port aux Basques and, of course, the $13 million St. John's harbour development. There can be no greater tribute to the tenure of office of the present Minister of Public Works, Mr. Chairman, than can be found in the estimates for the coming year.
In conclusion I should like also at this time to pay tribute to the hard working staff, the district engineer and the staff, of the Newfoundland region. Nowhere else in Canada do public works present such a challenge as in Newfoundland and, as I said before, nowhere else in Canada are public works so important.
I would recommend to the minister and to his officers that they bear this in mind when
tMr. McGrath.]

they view the various requests that come from time to time for additional staff. There have been additions to the staff of the Newfoundland office in recent months, but with all due respect I suggest that the staff of the Newfoundland office is still inadequate. They make up, perhaps, for lack of numbers in the quality of the personnel employed in the public works office in Newfoundland.

I feel that first I must express my personal regrets at the departure of the now acting Minister of Public Works from that post. I offer him my sincere congratulations upon his appointment to the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sure this house is of the belief that he will do his best in that important post, just as he has in the past during his term as Minister of Public Works. We all wish him every success. While not always agreeing with his decisions I must admit that I found the acting minister a very fair man in all his dealings. I now wish him well. I believe in sending flowers while the minister is alive and can smell them. I had hoped that he would remain in office until all the wharves in my riding had been constructed or repaired. I hope when his successor is appointed he will give a sympathetic hearing and reasonable consideration to the many requests which he is sure to receive from me from time to time.
I feel that I should also publicly pay tribute to the officials of the Department of Public Works in their sincere endeavour to do their best in the interests of all concerned at all times. I extend my sincere gratitude to all the officials.
In my riding of Trinity-Conception there are many fishing communities, some of which are very important because of the quantity of codfish produced and the many fish plants that are located there. I am glad the Department of Public Works has tried to assist the fishermen in these areas. For instance, at Harbour Grace approximately $136,000 has been spent during the past five years on harbour improvements for the benefit of the fishermen. At Catalina island, in the northern part of my riding, approximately $745,000 has been spent during the past five years. Approximately one-quarter of all the Newfoundland salt codfish is exported from the Catalina island area. A model fish plant is also located at this harbour and is operated by Fisheries Products Limited.
There is a large federal experimental salt fish drier at Catalina on the premises of S. W. Mifflin Limited. A dredging program was also carried out here, but more dredging is required to make it easier for ships to enter and leave the harbour. A coastal wharf has been built and now a fishermen's wharf is

being constructed. In the Bay de Verde and Port de Grave area the department has also spent much money during the past five years. These are two very important fishing centres, and we know these expenditures have been justified.
There are still, however, many more areas in which public works improvements would be of great economic benefit. Many of these areas have already been brought to the attention of the minister from time to time by way of petitions, letters and telephone calls, and I must say that I have received reports on all but, as may be expected, they have not always been favourable. For instance, last year I presented a petition to the Department of Public Works for a wharf at Dildo South, where there is a large whaling and fresh fish operation and from which point I believe the only mink feed delivery service in Canada operates, catering to some 25 mink ranchers in the Blaketown area. Last year about 25,000 mink pelts were produced, which brought some $500,000 to Newfoundland. However, more fresh fish is needed to provide additional feed for the mink. I understand the Department of Public Works, after making a careful survey, is considering the [DOT]construction of a wharf there. This will be [DOT]of great assistance to all the people in that general area.
There are many places where the fishermen have requested extensions to the present wharfing facilities. The following places come to mind: Britannia; Caplin Cove; Chance [DOT]Cove; Deer Harbour; Gooseberry Cove; Green's Harbour, eastern end; Heart's Desire; Lead Cove; Little Heart's Ease; New Harbour; Norman's Cove; Spaniard's Bay and Sunny-side. Requests have also been received for the construction of wharves from the following .settlements:	Bishop's Cove; Burnt Point;
Butter Cove; Grate's Cove; Green's Harbour, western end; Hillview; Harbour Grace south; Melrose; Monroe; Queen's Cove; Sunnyside; Thornlea and Winterton. Many of these requests were made last year, and I am sure The Department of Public Works will give them serious consideration.
When those wharves have been extended or constructed, Mr. Chairman, I shall have much pleasure in furnishing the names of other settlements which need public works attention. Once again I suggest that docking facilities be established at Harbour Grace and Clarenville in order to take care of the boats requiring docking facilities, because the Canadian National Railways dock at St. John's is not able to cater to the boats and schooners requiring its facilities.
A fishermen's landing is also badly needed in Carbonear, and I am hopeful that the
Supply-Public Works department will take care of that matter this year. I am convinced that the present plan for community stages should be continued, as I am sure they will prove to be extremely beneficial. I strongly suggest that, because of weather conditions, much of the public works construction be carried out in Newfoundland during the early spring or the late fall rather than in the winter months.
I believe the federal government should also give increased financial assistance to Newfoundland to complete the trans-Canada highway, because Newfoundland has not a standard gauge railway and consequently cannot cater to the trade of the province adequately and at competitive cost in any favourable proportion as compared with the situation in the other provinces of Canada. It is the duty of the federal government of Canada, to provide Newfoundland with a railway service in keeping with that in the rest of Canada, to keep the cost of the transportation of goods, etc. into and out of Newfoundland at the same level as in the other provinces. Consequently any extra financial assistance given to Newfoundland to complete her portion of the trans-Canada highway will only square up matters with the province of Newfoundland. Newfoundland then will not be receiving in proportion any more favourable treatment than that which the other provinces of Canada are receiving from the federal government.

Without unduly delaying the passage of the estimates I should like to be permitted at this time, on my own behalf, on behalf of the people of my constituency and of the people of the province of New Brunswick generally, to express to the Minister of Public Works our appreciation for what he has done for our province during his tenure of office. The universal approval of the announcement made yesterday indicates the cherished position he holds in this house, and I think that is the position he holds in the minds of the Canadian people generally.
For a long period of time the present Minister of Public Works has been held in very high esteem by the people of my province. I feel that I would be remiss in my duty as a member from that province if I did not convey to him at this time our feelings and our appreciation of what he has done for us. I should like also to convey on behalf of the people of my constituency, particularly the people of Campobello island, appreciation for his co-operation and for the assistance he has given to that part of New Brunswick.
The Minister of Public Works has brought to that department a realistic appreciation of the problems confronting the people of New

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My remarks will be brief and will be directed toward one aspect only of the minister's activities. However, before I embark upon them perhaps the committee will allow me to reiterate my congratulations to the minister on his appointment to this new and high office to which he has been called by the government. May I say to him that I am delighted that he will remain house leader for the rest of the session but that, on the other hand, I am sorry that because of the importance of his new duties he may not be able to carry on those duties during the following session in 1960. No one will miss him more than I. I am happy to say that during the time he has occupied that office of house leader our relationship has been of the happiest kind and certainly one of great co-operation.
I rose to speak about port development along the St. Lawrence. I am particularly interested in this matter not only because of my close association with it during the almost ten years in which I held the position of Minister of Transport and then in another position as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority for three years.
Again I want to bring to the attention of the minister and his officials the importance of adequate port facilities all along the seaway. It has been said repeatedly by economists that more money is now being spent by industry from the lower St. Lawrence right up to the head of the lakes for industrial development than on the seaway itself. If that is the case, and I believe it to be,
[Mr. Stewart.l

then it is of equal importance that the ports which come under the jurisdiction of the minister be adequately equipped.
I speak first of all, of course, of the ports in the province of Quebec. I am particularly interested in them. But before doing so I should like to remind the minister of a suggestion I made in 1957 and again in 1958 both to the Minister of Public Works and to the Minister of Transport, but to which apparently little or no heed was paid. Perhaps it was not thought to be important at the time. However, I believe circumstances have shown that it was important.
The recommendation I made was that a body be set up to make an economic survey of all the regions of the St. Lawrence seaway and how those regions would be affected, including the ports, from one end to the other. While I was not successful in 1957 in convincing the government that this was something that should be done, I was successful in getting a recommendation in the annual report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. While I do not have it available at the moment, and I do not want to delay these estimates, it is clearly a recommendation in the report of 1958 that an economic survey be made of all the regions and areas affected by the seaway.

Now I come back to these ports. I refer to Seven Islands, Baie Comeau, Ri-mouski and other such ports. I suggest that if private industry can go to the length of an expenditure of that nature-I have not the figure before me now but I know it is a matter of many millions of dollars-the Department of Public Works should give consideration to providing facilities at that fast-growing community.

speechtext:
Yes, I have, but I was wondering if the minister felt that was enough under the circumstances, because there will be great development in that area. I would say it is anticipated that there will be great development because of this increased movement and the fact that the ships will go from the head of the lakes now right down to Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports without transshipment. Therefore new, more modern and more up to date facilities are required at these ports; and while I have seen the minister's statement I was just wondering if that was going far enough.
I am going to curtail my remarks, but I do want to deal with the ports in the province of Ontario. I spoke at Port Arthur some weeks ago, and I was astounded to find that practically nothing had been done at the lakehead toward development. I know the minister has had a survey group look into the actual conditions and possible future harbour and other requirements along the St. Lawrence river as a result of the completion of the seaway, and one such group went to Cornwall, Belleville, Kingston, and other ports right up to Toronto.
There is quite a bit of discussion right now as to what should be done at the city of Cornwall, and I am sorry to say there is not nearly as much being done there as there should be. There are places, for instance like Kingston, that are complaining that they are off the beaten path, some distance away from the deep channel; but notwithstanding that, Kingston is going to become quite an important port for down river traffic. In fact one large corporation has already indicated its intention of making the city of Kingston a base for future developments.
What I am coming to now is this. Take a place like the city of Cornwall. That port is right on deep water. Both extremities have deep water facilities of over 27 feet, and can therefore take the 25J feet draft vessels. It seems to me that in the two years the government has been in office more attention should have been given to that community. I know that representations have been made by the hon. member for Stormont, but I am sure he will not mind my rising in the House of Commons at this time because of my close association with that community, and I do not rise for any other purpose than to be helpful. All I say is that there are all the facilities in the world, and I do wish the minister would give some special attention to that port.

On the whole I rose simply to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in the United States large sums of money are being spent in anticipation of future traffic, and it seems to me that we should be giving the same attention on this side of the international line.

I realize that the minister would appreciate getting his estimates through this committee as expeditiously as possible. We wish to assist him in that regard, so I will take only a very brief period of the time of this committee.
However, I wish to express my appreciation, and the appreciation of the constituents of Moose Jaw city, to the minister with regard to the construction of our new federal building which was made possible by the hon. gentleman's decision shortly after he assumed office as Minister of Public Works. The new federal building in Moose Jaw is now rising rapidly and will be open early next year. The final vote for $600,000 for the completion of the building appears in the estimates before us. Last year there was a vote of $500,000 for the new building, and newspapers give some idea of its proportions.
Moose Jaw city has been built up very greatly in the last two years, particularly in the northwest and southwest areas, and I contend that this is due very largely to the housing program of the Department of Public Works. The minister can be very proud of the success of his efforts in this regard, and I trust that his successor in the department will follow his fine example.
Through the fortunes of constituency redistribution I also represent the outer-the growing-areas of Regina city, and here, also, the minister's housing program has been the means of very rapid expansion. I know his efforts, and the efforts of his department, are very greatly appreciated. At the present time there is a program for a large rental housing project in north Regina an area which, as I said, is included in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. I have had something to do with the arrangements for this proposed project and I hope the minister will be in a position to make a definite announcement in the near future.
Of course, as a Moose Jaw resident I will draw the minister's attention to the need for further extensions of this program in Moose

Supply-Public Works
Jaw. There are other items included in these estimates dealing with repairs and improvements to various public buildings in Saskatchewan. Some of these buildings are, I am sure, in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. We welcome this extra work and this indication of the minister's continued interest on our behalf.
Before I resume my seat I wish to take this opportunity to offer my personal congratulations and the congratulations of the people of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre to the minister upon his appointment as Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sure that after all the statements which have been made by previous speakers, all of which I endorse wholeheartedly, the minister will know that he has the best wishes of all members and of Canadian people in his new call to service for Canada. We can rest assured that the external affairs of this country are in good hands. Once again, while he is still Minister of Public Works I wish to thank the hon. gentleman on behalf of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre for the co-operation he has always given us in tackling our problems, particularly our housing problems.

In common with most hon. members I am very interested in the estimates of the Department of Public Works. I come from a riding where most of the people live in seaport towns or small outport settlements and their interest in marine works in particular is very keen indeed.
I should like for a moment to talk about the value of small works in such places as these, places where very often the sea is the highway and the boat and the wharf take the place of the car and the road. Most of these places are fishing settlements and some of these settlements are exposed; they are not all built in good harbours; they are built in shallow coves where some improvement on nature is necessary if the fishermen are to pursue their vocation over a period of reasonable length.
In some of these fishing settlements a small breakwater can make all the difference between a short fishing season and a long one, or between a fishing season which is constant and one which is interrupted by storms which compel fishermen to haul up their boats. Small breakwaters, not costing very much money in some instances, can make half decent small harbours; practical harbours where boats can remain at anchor during a storm.
Then there are places where for physical and economic reasons breakwaters are not practicable. In such places, small slipways, complete with either power winches or hand winches could be utilized for hauling boats
IMr. Pascoe.]
out of the water rapidly when storms approach and then enabling them to be launched fairly quickly when the sea is again fit for fishing.
Then there is the small landing wharf. Apart from being a place where boats may tie up and the catch may be landed these wharfs become a focal point for fishing activities and, in many cases, they are used for purposes far beyond the original intention of the wharf. They are used to dry nets, to handle fish and to land supplies. Many of these small wharves cost very little and the funds for their construction come out of the miscellaneous or general vote. It is for this reason that I should like to suggest that the minister consider enlarging this miscellaneous vote so as to take care of a greater number of these small marine activities.
The community stages program which began last year will, without doubt, become one of the very best programs thus far instituted for the benefit of fishermen. Just as the small public wharf becomes a focal point for fishermen, so on a larger and more efficient scale is the community stage for the whole fishing community and I do hope that this program will be extended and, if possible, enlarged.
While I do not think I should attempt to name here all the places where community stages should be built, I should like to suggest that St. Anthony, one of the most important fishing towns in the north does need something in the way of community stages. I do not think one community stage would be sufficient there owing to the layout of the town. Two or three should be considered.
I should like to speak briefly about one or two larger projects. Before doing so I should like to thank the minister for the program which has been instituted this year in my riding calling for the completion of the wharf at Battle Harbour, Sop's Arm; the important wharf at Goose Bay mentioned this morning by my colleague the hon. member for St. John's East; and at Hampden, Harbour Round and Ming's Bight and Williams Harbour on the Labrador. I understand, too, the department will be lengthening and enlarging the Canadian National Railways docks at Lewisporte.
All these are vitally needed. I do not want to appear to be greedy and simply say that "these things ought ye to have done and not to have left the other undone". I am very pleased that these projects are being built this year. I do hope, however, that special attention can be given to the port of Botwood this year. This is an important point of shipping for central Newfoundland.

For several years the people of Botwood have urged the construction of a public wharf for their seaport town.
There are some places along the coast of the Labrador where small wharves are necessary. There are places like Baie Verte in Newfoundland, where the asbestos mines are being developed and where a large coastal wharf is needed. I may perhaps be forgiven for calling attention to Woodstock. In connection with this place it was pointed out by the department that it not being a port of call for the C.N.R. steamers a coastal wharf was not necessary. While the C.N.R. pointed out that there not being a wharf at Woodstock, their steamers could not make it a port of call. Within the next twelve months I hope there is sufficient co-operation between the department and the other organization so that some consideration may be given to co-ordinating the building and completion of the wharf with the calling of the steamer.
With respect to public buildings I should like to repeat what I said once before. Small public buildings, even as large public buildings are monuments to Canada. This should be kept in mind when they are being designed. I do not suggest that buildings as large or as ornate as the parliament buildings should be built in small towns but I do suggest that when a building is designed it should adequately portray what Canada is. It should be neat, attractive, well proportioned and adequate and should be designed to house all federal government services in the community.
To illustrate my point I shall refer to Glenwood to which reference has already been made. A post office is badly needed in Glenwood. The Canadian National Telegraphs is putting in a new telephone system which will require a building. Unless there is proper liaison between the two bodies the C.N.T. will have its own small building and the post office will have its own small building. We will have two small buildings, when instead we could have a larger and better building that would be a credit to Canada and honour the name it will bear. At the same time it would be more economical.
I feel rather strongly about the value of these buildings in terms of the impression they create on people in the community and particularly young people who grow up and form their impressions of Canada from the type of buildings on which they see that proud name written.
I should also like to mention the buildings which are nearing completion in St. John's. The customs building and the post office building are both nearing completion. My
66968-9-278
Supply-Public Works understanding is that the previous administration had a program of building to follow the completion of these structures so that employment would be maintained at a reasonable level. There were to be fisheries, transport and unemployment insurance buildings. As we near completion of the buildings now under construction I trust that the department has in mind plans for future building.
It is a matter of personal pride for me to know that harbour developments are getting well along at St. John's. I supported that development last year and perhaps I may be pardoned for saying that this was planned under the previous administration.
I wish to repeat that a large miscellaneous vote is important. Small wharves, breakwaters, slipways and winches are all vitally important to the development of our fisheries and to the provision of a constant source of employment to those who are engaged in the fishing industry.
I should like to conclude by offering my sincere congratulations to the minister on his new appointment. My pleasure is somewhat tinged with regret because he is leaving the Department of Public Works. I am sure he will bring to his new duties the same spirit of fairness and dedication he has displayed in his present position. I wish also to pay tribute to the officials of his department who year after year work constantly and steadily in the interests of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege for me to have the opportunity of paying a tribute to the new Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of the people of St. Boniface. Yesterday the hon. member for York-Scarborough paid tribute to the minister on behalf of the people in his corner and at this time I should like to pay the same tribute on behalf of those in this corner. This may not be the most privileged part of the house but we in this part of the chamber feel that the minister has been more or less a father to us all.
Sometimes we feel jealous of the opposition parties who are given greater privileges than are we who are members of the Conservative party and who sit in this remote corner of the house but we know this is done because the minister is a great lover of the freedom of parliament and he is really letting hon. members of the opposition parties have as much rope as possible. However, knowing what use they have made of the rope, we also feel the minister has a great love for us in this corner.
I should also like to thank the minister who is also deputy premier and leader of

Supply-Public Works the house for the great benefits that the people of St. Boniface have received since this party came to office. St. Boniface, which is the most important French-speaking city west of the Ottawa river, has been given a satellite television station. It has been given also a channel of equal importance to that given to the English-speaking Canadians. On behalf of the 68,000 French-speaking people of Manitoba, and I might say also on behalf of the four million French-speaking people of Canada, I thank the minister and the present government.
The present minister has the reputation of a man of integrity and of action. One of the great things he has done has been in connection with national housing. Many of those houses have been constructed in Manitoba, but I deplore the fact that none of the minimum cost houses has yet been constructed there. It is not the minister's fault. I believe this plan should be advertised more and I am sure that if minimum cost houses are being provided for the people of Canada it is because the minister feels for the people of less wealth. I believe it is a great thing for them.
I am sorry to see the minister go, but I should like to leave some observations with him regarding national housing. This week
1	received a plan design having to do with Canada's first family H-bomb shelter in connection with civil defence. It is called "The Telegram Family H-Bomb Shelter" for individual dwellings designed in collaboration with civil defence headquarters. I would greatly appreciate it if under national housing a few of the houses were constructed with a shelter and advertised to see what kind of demand there would be for houses with a shelter constructed in the plan. I know there is a great difference of opinion among people generally regarding civil defence. I believe that some leadership should be given by the government. Since the government is interested in the construction of houses for people, they should set the example by constructing a few houses at the start with a shelter. We know that in Sweden no one can construct a dwelling unless he first obtains a permit. He has to agree to spend at least
2	per cent of the value of the dwelling upon a shelter. If this is feasible, knowing the present minister is a man of action, I know that before he leaves his department he will do something in this connection. Thank you.

I want to join with other hon. members who have spoken so far in this debate to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the high assignment which has been imposed upon him by the Prime Minister. I wish him well in his new portfolio.


My first remarks, Mr. Chairman, on the first item of the public works estimates will be very short. I have two or three questions which I wish to ask the minister, and I am seeking information. First, I should like to know from the minister what decision has been taken with regard to my repeated requests and demands for improvement to the present wharf at Maisonnette? Maisonnette is one of the many fishing communities in my constituency. It is a small bay, a shelter, where we have over 40 fishing boats. Those fishermen are in urgent need of more improvements. Their landings last year amounted to over 1J million pounds of fish. Their present facilities are definitely inadequate. I hope that the request and the demands from the Maisonnette fishermen, which I have placed before the department on many occasions, will be looked at favourably.
Another project which is urgently needed in my constituency is an improvement to the Tracadie gully. The entrance to that gully is practically blocked off by an old, partially demolished breakwater which is a menace to navigation and to the safety of the fishermen. Last year I was notified by the Department of Public Works that the national research council was to undertake a study to determine what could be done to improve the entrance to the Tracadie gully. I would like to know the results of this study? I was also notified by the department that a hydrographic survey was to be undertaken during the present summer, the 1959 season. I should also like to know from the minister what has been done so far to carry out this survey. I know the fishermen of the area are asking that a small causeway be built between Ferguson gully and Tracadie gully. I am inclined to agree with the fishermen that it would improve the entrance to both gullys, which I understand have been a problem to the engineers of the department.
The last question which I would like to ask the minister is what is the situation with regard to the request which has been received for a public building in the town of Shippegan? The present facilities, providing space for the post office and for the three or four offices of the Department of Fisheries, are definitely inadequate. Representations have been made by the town council of Shippegan and by the local chamber of commerce. I should like to know what progress has been made or whether a decision has been reached by the department to provide the town of Shippegan with an adequate public building?
I wish to close my short remarks. I may have one or two small questions to ask on the

different items later on. I should like the minister to give us information on the three points I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment as Secretary of State for External Affairs. (Translation):
It is an honour that redounds to his family, his constituency and the whole of Canada. I am convinced that he will be a credit to his country and will be one of the most prominent men of our international life.
Mr. Chairman, at one time the federal government would build retaining walls along river banks. That practice was discontinued a few years ago.
I have here numerous requests made by the city of Joliette and neighbouring communities, as well as from the city of L'Assomption and from the municipalities of L'Epiphanie and Charlemagne, asking for the construction of retaining walls in order to protect public buildings such as colleges, convents or properties with river frontage.
I should be very glad, if at all possible, to know the exact reason why the government decided in the past to discontinue such a policy.
