I do not intend to long delay the estimates of the minister, but I should like to discuss two or three particular topics at this time. In the northern part of Newfoundland, north of Flower's Cove, in the straits of Belle Isle, there is a large concentration of population in seven or eight settlements. In only one of these settlements so far have we been able to provide any marine construction. Those people who live on this section of the Newfoundland coast are the people who are engaged in the cod fishery and because of the prevailing weather and the distances from the fishing grounds, they must use fairly large and fairly heavy boats. These people who live in these settlements have no protection for these boats. When storms are coming they must of necessity have these boats hauled up and the next morning they have to launch them again. Obviously, a great deal of time is lost in doing this. One can understand, too, that at times these men lose a great deal of their equipment. I have corresponded with the minister about a number of these places and I should like to urge now on behalf of these people that consideration be given to their needs.
Coming farther south along the west coast of Newfoundland, there is an island known as St. John island. This island, for a number of years, has been the site of a large lobster 66968-9-2781
Supply-Public Works pool. The fishermen in St. John bay have now decided that they want to build a fishing establishment on this island, because part of the island has a fairly good harbour protected from the spring ice floes and from the prevailing storms. They, of their own accord and at their own expense, have provided the timber. They have had it cut and landed on site to provide the inshore establishment that will be required. They have been able to provide everything for themselves except a wharf. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that industry of this type on the part of people who want to help themselves should be rewarded. I believe, too, that they should not only be rewarded for their own work but also for the fact that industry in this particular section in which they are engaged will, I believe, turn out to be economically sound. I would hope the minister would give consideration to building a St. John island wharf that would be suitable for the use of the fishermen who will be using this island during the fishing season.
May I make a reference at this time to another fishing settlement on the west coast of Newfoundland known as Parson's Pond. Parson's Pond is a fairly large settlement as fishing villages on the west coast go, and it is composed of a fairly large number of very industrious men. The problem that exists there is, in all probability, not a very simple one. Some dredging is needed and there is cribwork needed around the small harbour itself, as well as a fishermen's wharf-
Two or three years ago the provincial government built a road down through this section which goes across Parson's Pond and it was necessary to build a temporary bridge at that time. I made inquiries of the minister and he replied that further consideration would be given to construction work at Parson's Pond when he could determine what effect this bridge would have on the flow of water from Parson's Pond out to the sea. During the coming season a permanent bridge will be built and I would think there would be sufficient information now to enable a determination to be made of the effect this bridge would have. I would recommend that the minister give very careful consideration to the possibility of marine construction at Parson's Pond.
Farther south along the west coast of Newfoundland we come to the very historic harbour of St. George's. This harbour is formed by a sandy bank which goes out from the mainland and forms a settlement known as Sandy Point. In the last four or five years storms have broken through Sandy Point and as a result what formerly formed the harbour of St. George's is now being

Supply-Public Works gradually washed away. I fear that if this is allowed to continue, in time not only will the harbour of St. George's be destroyed but there will also be a tremendous effect on the fisheries that are carried on in that particular area. I believe that the job of preventing any further erosion now would not be very expensive, but as time goes on and the gap at Sandy Point gets bigger and bigger, Sandy Point will become nothing but an island. In the long run this will be detrimental to the people of St. George's, and the harbour which has been a shelter for ships for so many years.
Last year the minister was able to initiate construction work at Codroy. I visited the settlement in the fall and I saw the work going on there. A good job was being done. I am sorry it was not possible for the company that was given this contract to resume work at an earlier period this year. During the past few months we have had particularly good weather in that section, and I believe a good deal of work could have been provided for the people if the company had decided to go ahead with the construction earlier in the year. I know there are some particular difficulties in the way here, but I would hope construction of these harbour facilities at Codroy would be resumed at the earliest possible date.
I have said before, Mr. Chairman, and I repeat that public works are particularly important in Newfoundland. I think that one thing that is of real importance is that these public works be started as early as possible in the year. The people who live in the Codroy area now are people who over the last five or six months have had no opportunity to earn any money. The result is that those who were dependent on the construction of Codroy harbour and those who were hoping to use this harbour for fishing are finding that the going is a little difficult. If this construction had been started earlier in the year it would have been possible for some men to get employment and possibly also for the fishermen to use what would be there. I would hope that this construction would be started as early as possible because it affects, not only the people in my riding but also a large number of people who live in the constituency of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. As in many places in Newfoundland, harbour construction very seldom concerns the one place where construction is to be completed; it also concerns many small places in a certain area. Codroy is a very good example of that.
I have had some correspondence with the minister concerning a peninsula on the west coast of Newfoundland known as Port au


Port peninsula. The people who live there are essentially fishermen. Years ago they were engaged almost 100 per cent in the fishery, but with the coming of the United States air force at Stephenville a number of these men sought work in the construction of this base. Many of them have remained there. While a great many men are able to find jobs at the United States air force base at Stephenville, there are still many more who have to find employment in some other way. Those who live on the Port au Port peninsula must, of necessity, find employment in the fishing industry. I have forwarded to the minister a list of settlements on the Port au Port peninsula which are in urgent need of some marine construction. In fact, I think in one of my letters to the minister I recommended that a survey be made of the whole peninsula to determine what could be done to encourage the fishermen in the trade which they have followed for so long. I hope that the minister will be able to give consideration to these particular places. The time may come-and I know we all hope so-when maybe the world will be in such a position that we shall no longer need these air force bases. When that time comes the great centre of employment for people in this area will have been taken away, and these people will be obliged to go back to fishing.
I would suggest to the minister that careful consideration be given to this matter when construction in the various settlements in the Port au Port peninsula are being considered. A community stage program is one which I think has a great deal of merit. I know that at the moment it is only in the experimental stage. However, from what has been done so far and from the information which the minister has been able to gather, I believe that he or his successor will be able to carry on this program. Port au Port would be one place in Newfoundland-there are others, of course-where this program could well be applied.
Finally, I should like to extend to the minister my personal congratulations on his being appointed Secretary of State for External Affairs and also to extend to him my personal good wishes. I know that not only will he represent Canada with dignity and diligence but also that in the councils of the world he will earn for himself that personal respect which his own country has accorded to him.

Mr. Chairman, may I also extend my congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sure that

he will bring to his new post the same dignity and savoir faire which he has brought to the portfolio of public works.
On several occasions I have made requests to the Department of Public Works, drawing to their attention the state of affairs that exists in the Magdalen islands with regard to the need for harbours and port facilities. For many years politicians have promised the construction of harbours or wharves here and there. Being one who never makes a promise except that of representing the people to the best of my ability, I do not believe that I have failed in bringing this matter to the attention of the Department of Public Works. Unfortunately, until this year few of the projects had been realized. We are grateful to the Department of Public Works for sending to the islands in October last a team of experts from the Department of Public Works as well as the Department of Transport who have, I believe, prepared a report which is quite favourable to the request of the people of my riding.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the lot of the fisherman is a hard one. He is subject to the whims and fancies of nature over which he has no control. However, we must bear in mind the fact that he can control the port facilities so that he may be able to approach the shores or leave the shores. Can you imagine that in this age a fisherman who has no land whatever is obliged to buy a 1,600 pound horse, that he is obliged to feed it and acquire the necessary gear to attach to his boat in order to haul his boat off the sands into four feet of water. If the least adverse condition makes it impossible, then the fisherman must spend his day^ on the sand watching others get their day's catch. This necessarily creates much wear and tear on the boat and the cost of maintenance is exorbitant.
We know that this is 1959. We cannot conceive of a situation where methods of one hundred years ago are still in use. No one can believe that a fisherman should subject himself to such slavery. Personally, I believe it is incomprehensible. To raise their boats on the slips or to have their boats thrown on the shore are not conditions consonant with the expectations of this era. I could name places like Etang des Caps, Millerand basin and Oyster basin which are places that have been studied by the officials of the Department of Public Works. These places definitely need quick consideration and development. There is a loss in production which runs into thousands of dollars. There is the physical slavery of those who must pursue that trade.
I know it is the desire of all Canadians to alleviate the sufferings of those who are
Supply-Public Works less fortunate than themselves. I am sure that the expenditure of the money that would be required could be easily justified. Economically speaking that may not be so. However, these are circumstances in which I do not believe we should consider only the economic advantage but rather the survival of twelve thousand people who wish to pursue their trade as it is the only one they know.
In the report that has been made by the department I understand that some of the projects are subject to study by the national research council. For this fact we are grateful to the government. We know that in the future no money will be spent haphazardly but that after consideration of the locality and construction a project will be built which will give long service to the people using it. I trust that the minister will take into consideration the fact that, although many requests are being made throughout the country for the study of projects by the national research council, these people who are fishermen-and fishing is their only means of livelihood-will get, not a preference above all other projects but a fair chance of having some of these projects studied.
In conclusion may I suggest this to the Minister of Public Works before he takes off on his world tours or to meet other people. I invite him down to the Magdalen islands on the week end to see some of these spots. I am sure that the scene which would meet his eyes there would touch a soft spot in his heart and result in bringing to these people the needed facilities.

I am sure the minister does not want to deprive me of an opportunity of making a few observations on the first item on his estimates. Perhaps if some of the other hon. gentlemen would like to make their speeches first I could sit down and allow them to do so. The minister will recall that a year ago I took him on a tour around my constituency and that tour was to a very limited degree fruitful. I think perhaps he has lost his chance to visit Newfoundland now he has moved into higher spheres. Incidentally I do not intend to join others in their obituaries of the minister. I will wait until the flowers really are needed. In the interval I suspect the minister will go on being a politician and I want to keep my hands clean so I can attack him whenever I wish; but that is irrelevant, sir.
I feel that the minister ought to take another tour around the coast of Newfoundland, especially around those beautiful coasts north of Bonavista which was first discovered by Cabot in 1497. That, I might remind the minister, was the beginning of the British empire to which he has always been so much

Supply-Public Works attached. We could end up in Twillingate and have the best lobsters in the world if he could come right away quickly while still Minister of Public Works and on the way he could authorize a lot of wharves, breakwaters and post offices. But I will make a deal with the minister. This is one of the deals one makes which are open and aboveboard. It is open to diplomacy, openly arrived at-I hope. I make the offer to the minister that if he will undertake to draw my speech of last year to the attention of his successor-who I dare say will be the hon. member for Montreal St. James, who is so well qualified for that post-and will get his secretary first to scratch out the few places where something has been done, then I will not make the speech again today. I wonder if the minister would like to reply to that? Of course, I have not finished.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, being still a politician, as the hon. member says, I have to be a little careful about these promises. However, I will be very glad to draw that to the attention of the new minister.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few things to add this year. There is one thing I would like the minister to tell me when he replies, and that is whether the department has in fact any plans for developing a slipway at Bonavista about which there had been a good deal of talk at one time or another in the press. I would also like to add my support to the appeal made by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador for an increase in the vote for small works. These works are very, very valuable, out of all proportion to their cost. I would like to ask the minister, who is now going to become a real elder statesman and perhaps will be able to look at these problems as a whole and transcend that endless quarrel between the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General about who is responsible for the little post offices, to direct his statesmanlike mind to this question in the future and see if something could not be done for the small places where there are no premises to rent and where the kind of post offices which exist at present are really no credit to Canada at all, and see if, even though the revenues may not be very great, something can be done about them.
I would just remind the minister that the nature of the problem is this, that where the old Newfoundland government had a post office the department will replace it always without question. But where a place has grown large since that time, although the revenues in that place may come to be higher than the revenues of many of the places which were large at an earlier stage, the

department has always applied the mainland rule and said that nothing would be done. This is impossible to explain to any Newfoundlander and I think it is an antiquated rule that, after ten years, ought to be abolished. I am not mentioning any of the places where I would like to see these buildings constructed because the minister has them in his files. There is only one single work I do especially want to ask the minister to commend to his successor, and that is the extension to the wharf at Newman's Cove. This has been on my conscience because it was in the program while we were still in office and it did not get done in 1957, and for one reason or another it has not been completed since. This is a very important fishing settlement where the fishery is growing and it really does need special attention. Beyond that, as I say, having lost my schooner on the very night I made that voyage around the coast last year, I hesitated to make the voyage this year and I thank the minister for what he said to save the voyage.
There is just one other thing I cannot refrain from putting on the record. Not long ago I had a letter from the chairman of a public meeting of the citizens of Dead-man's Bay, and there is just one paragraph I would like the minister to commend to his successor. I will not read any of the critical parts of this letter, but I think this part ought to be on the record as a guide for the future. This is a description of what happened when we were in office. This gentleman says:
When the Liberals had to share it-
That is to say, the labour of public works-
-every man had his part. It was all shared alike both work and sticks.
I hope that will be done too by the minister's successor.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, no matter who the minister may be, and I mean including myself, this discussion has been very helpful to the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Cannot you give us some idea?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Considering the estimates is a very useful way of finding out what improvements can be made in the work of the department. My experience with the Department of Public Works has convinced me that it is an extremely efficient department, trying to do a job for the Canadian people. While in opposition I had the responsibility of criticizing the department from time to time, and in that way gained quite a good idea of how it functioned. I would like to

repeat again today my great admiration for the work done by my predecessor, the Hon. Robert Winters, and the deputy he took with him from his former department, Major General Hugh Young, who is still the deputy of the department. They with other officials have built up an excellent team with an excellent team spirit, and it has been one of the most pleasant jobs I have ever undertaken in my life to work with them in this department. I am sure that hon. members will find that the same attitude and the same efficiency will be shown by the department in the years which lie ahead.
After all, it is the great building department of the government services and as one hon. member said last night there will be a steadily increasing amount of work to be done. I believe that future construction by the federal government will be in excellent hands as long as the department is managed as it has been by the present officials.
I do not intend to thank hon. members again for their words of encouragement to myself. I did that yesterday. But I should like to say that I have never felt so humble as I do now having listened to all those words of praise. Last evening I got a message from my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration pointing out she could not recognize who he was they were speaking about. I must admit I felt very much the same way.
I cannot deal with all the points which have been raised by hon. members, but I should like to deal with some of them briefly beginning with the remarks made by my old friend, the hon. member for Levis. I may tell him that in the department he is considered as a fine member with whom to work and as a great friend. I would have expected that from my association with him down through the years and that is his reputation in the Department of Public Works today, after the splendid work he did as parliamentary assistant.
The hon. member commented on the fact that the estimates of the department this year are lower than they were last year. That, of course, is true, but when one takes into account the increase in the construction work being done by this department for other departments the actual money which will be spent will be almost as much as in the last fiscal year. The hon. member knows that it is not always easy to get over the hurdles placed by the treasury board. I am learning to have considerable respect for that august body. They really did very well for the department this year in view of the fact that taxes were being raised and there were many other problems to be faced.
Supply-Public Works
Then the hon. member referred to the fact that we had not spent as large a percentage of the vote during the last fiscal year as had been spent in the year 1957-58. One very good reason for this was the severe weather during this last winter. That has handicapped the department in a good many of its projects. Then the hon. member asked about a possible conference with the provinces to discuss a new highway program upon the expiry of the present agreement. That agreement continues until the end of 1960, and there is no intention of calling such a conference during the present calendar year. I have had useful discussions with some of the provincial ministers. Last week I met with the minister of highways for Saskatchewan and the minister of public works for Manitoba. All the provincial governments are very much interested in what the policy of the federal government is to be, and I am hoping that next year it will be possible to clarify the situation. It is a little difficult, as I do not see how there can be such a clear-cut policy as the trans-Canada highway policy-the situation is so different in the different provinces. Possibly some policy may have to be adopted which will allow one type of aid in one province and another type of aid in another province in order to serve the national interest. We are, however, very much aware of a need for a decision on this question.
Then the hon. member for Kootenay West had several very useful suggestions to make. He emphasized the need for planning ahead and, of course, that is essential, particularly in a building department of the type of the Department of Public Works. There is a very good economics branch in the department and very useful work is being done in planning projects. Of course, efficiency can always be increased, but I think the department is doing very good work in this regard.
The hon. member also suggested that officials of the department should go around and speak at different centres across the country. That idea has considerable merit, although, like politicians, officials of the department could get into trouble by saying the right thing at the wrong time or vice versa. I do not know just how far a policy of that kind could be followed, but I do agree that good public relations are essential, and I think that is what the hon. member had in mind. He suggested, for example, that the local papers should be informed of plans involving their communities. This would be very helpful and we shall see what we can do along these lines.

What I particularly had in mind with respect to senior officials was something strictly non-contentious, a subject
4386	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works for example, such as "your federal department of public works and its organization". I was thinking that when it was convenient, and when the officials were in these areas, they might address rotary clubs or chambers of commerce or organizations of that kind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, those suggestions will be given mature consideration.
I do not intend to deal with the questions which have been raised on housing. They can be covered when we come to the items submitted on behalf of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. But I do appreciate the comments which have been made by various hon. members.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo had some interesting suggestions to make. He wondered why we let out the hauling of rocks by contract rather than engage people to do it. I am not sure whether I shall be able to follow out the suggestion he made, but we will consider it. He commented on the reduction in expenditure on buildings in Newfoundland. This is because the two large buildings in St. John's are practically complete. These big buildings are the ones that cost the large sums of money. The cost of 15 or 20 small buildings would be equal to the cost of one large one.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador said he thought there had been a plan for a succession of government buildings in St. John's once the two now under construction are completed. We are endeavouring to make the necessary arrangements for a building for the unemployment insurance commission but sufficient progress has not yet been made to go ahead with that building. The officials are not aware of a plan for a succession of buildings in that city.
What about the fisheries building? That certainly was under discussion when we were in office.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that building is to be paid for by the Department of Fisheries and we are to build it. It should have been included in my remarks as a building to be constructed shortly.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam advocated the establishment of a Fraser river authority to supervise the development of that great river. An attempt is being made to further the co-operation of the different bodies involved with the river but at the moment there is no plan for an overriding authority. That may come eventually but there would be many difficulties to be ironed out before a movement of that kind could be made.
The hon. member for Lincoln suggested that there should be a new war museum.
[Mr. Herridge.l

I heartily agreed with that comment but unfortunately that comes under the Department of National Defence so we cannot do very much about it. He also referred to the temporary buildings in the capital city. That again is a difficult problem. The policy for some years has been to build permanent buildings just as quickly as possible but the government can go only as far as the funds permit and I believe we have to have a sense of proportion and distribute the money that is available, to the extent that can be done, fairly across the country. It is very tempting to build these wonderful new buildings in Ottawa right away or just as fast as possible but experience dictates that one has to go a step at a time. Eventually all the temporary buildings will be replaced.
The hon. member for Hull mentioned the need for another bridge across the river. I agree with him that this need exists. There have been difficulties in reaching agreement as to the financing for such a bridge. It would be interprovincial and I think everyone would agree that the three governmental bodies should join in the erection of such a bridge. At the moment I cannot give the hon. member any idea as to when this objective may be attained but I shall see to it that my successor is made aware of the need for such a structure.
The hon. member for Gaspe spoke of the needs of his constituency. He happens to have one of those ridings which has a very long coastline like the ridings in Newfoundland and along the west coast. We are trying to provide harbour improvements there as quickly as possible and considerable progress has been made. I must say he is a very persistent advocate of work in that riding. In fact, I find that most hon. members are becoming steadily better at the business of urging that things be done in their constituencies.
So was the previous hon. member for Gaspe.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Of course, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is a past master in this particular type of undertaking. I was somewhat afraid that he was going to take me on another tour of his riding. Perhaps that is the reason I met his request so quickly.
The hon. member for Halifax pointed out the need for consideration being given to paraplegics when constructing public buildings. I agree with his suggestion. We have just recently changed the entrance to the new public building being erected in Souris, Prince Edward Island. The officials assure me they will do the best they can to see that these

Canadians are not handicapped because of the type of entrances placed on public buildings.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi felt there had not been sufficient money spent in his constituency but I would remind him that we have just finished a public building in Newcastle which cost nearly $350,000.
Built by the former government, I might add.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, we put up practically all the money.
The contract was awarded before the election.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we have done fairly well in this respect.
Have you named it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member also referred to the bridge over the Miramichi at Chatham and wanted to know what the policy of the government is with regard to that bridge. He quoted from what I believe is his family's newspaper. In any event it is a good newspaper and the paper quoted my remarks at some length for which I am grateful. The situation there is that this bridge is not on the trans-Canada highway and there is no basis at the present time on which the federal government could share in the costs. However, under a highway policy to follow the completion of the trans-Canada highway policy this bridge would be covered if the particular highway were made part of the system which was to receive assistance from the federal government.
This is what I pointed out to the committee which met me while I was campaigning without much success in this riding a little over a year ago. I have not had a delegation from the riding visit me here. I took it from the hon. gentleman's remarks that he was under the impression that such a delegation had been here but I think that was wrong.

If I may interrupt with the minister's permission I would like to say that I quoted from the Chatham newspaper, the Gazette. I have no connection whatever with the paper, not that I would be averse to having the minister quoted at length in any paper with which I were connected.
I tried to point out to the minister at that time that I felt-and I think he will find it in Hansard-the reporter who covered the meeting was a little over-optimistic in what the minister said. I share the minister's view that the provincial government is responsible for the bridge until such time as a road is built which becomes a section of the trans-Canada highway.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member referred to a proposed road running from Quebec through Maine into New Brunswick. The officials of the department have no knowledge of any such projected road. He also mentioned Shediac.

A tourist wharf. Perhaps I can tell the minister that it was a meeting of the town council and the provincial secretary-treasurer of the province of New Brunswick said that in regard to the proposal the federal government would share up to the amount of $130,000 in the construction of a tourist wharf.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
With respect to the proposed tourist wharf at Shediac, the town authorities and the provincial government have presented a proposal to the department whereby the construction of a wharf to improve facilities for the tourist industry might be undertaken on a shared cost basis. Our officials have carried out an investigation and the estimated cost of a suitable structure would be in the neighbourhood of $160,000 to $175,000. There is no doubt that Shediac is a very popular resort area, and tourism plays a big part in the economic life of this community. There is a small element of fishery involved as well. However, to date the department has not completed its examination of this proposal, so that no decision has been reached.
The hon. member also referred to some employees on a government dredge whom he said had been dismissed. There were no employees dismissed. There were no employees whose terms of employment were terminated. I must make it perfectly clear that employees on the dredges are hired for the summer. When they finish the work they have not any right to consider that they are entitled to come back again the next spring. In many cases they have been rehired, but there is absolutely no right to this. I really think that the members of the opposition have not very much complaint against me for the way in which I treated employees who were in the employ of the department before we took office. There might be more cause for complaint from this side of the house on that score.
I was interested in the statement made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when he read from a letter. I have been saving a letter of reference for nearly a year. This is from Wreck Cove, Nova Scotia dated December 27, 1958.
How do you spell the name?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is Wreck Cove, Nova Scotia. I do not know whether this is a name for the hon. member or not. The letter is addressed to:
4388	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works Mr. Robert Muir, M.P.,
Sydney Mines.
Nova Scotia.
Dear Sir:
The work at the shore at Wreck Cove which has been under way since November 10, is just about completed.
If there had been any discrimination in connection with the employing of men on this project, you would have been advised of same before now. So. since there was none, I think it only fair to advise you accordingly.
This work, under the foremanship of Alex Smith, has been carried on in a very fair manner. All the available men in a given area were employed on this project without any consideration as to political affiliations.
We want you to know, as well as Mr. Smith, that we deeply appreciate the fairness shown in employing men at Wreck Cove.
Wishing you the compliments of the season, I am
Yours truly,
Norman J. MacAskill
President, Victoria County Liberal Association.
It is really dangerous to read that letter in the committee but I did so simply to prove that while we may not have been perfect, we have done pretty well.
The hon. member for Trinity-Conception said he wished me to smell the flowers while I was still able to do so. I greatly appreciate that remark. He also dealt with the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland. I agree that there is a special problem in that province in connection with this highway, a problem which will have to be dealt with as a separate one.
The hon. member for Charlotte spoke of the Campobello-Lubec bridge. As he pointed out, the governor of Maine has now signed a bill authorizing that state to participate; therefore, we shall be getting ahead with the construction in the very near future. The real credit for this bridge goes not to the Minister of Public Works, but to the hon. member himself who has been most helpful and, of course, most persistent in getting action on this bridge.
The hon. member for Laurier raised a very important problem in connection with the opening of the seaway and the development of the lower St. Lawrence river. We all realized that the seaway would bring tremendous changes to this part of Canada; in fact, to a very large part of Canada, but I do not think any of us realized just how extensive those changes would be. The department has done a great deal in the way of making plans for new harbours, various other projects and in the lower St. Lawrence, but I have reached the conclusion that a great deal more will have to be done. This seaway development is going to be of even greater importance than most of us expected.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to advise the minister that his time has expired, but I assume the committee will give him unanimous consent to continue.
For the last time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very grateful to hon. members for giving me extra time. We have an excellent team in the government service which was set up, incidentally, by my predecessor, a team consisting of officials from the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works, and on occasion representatives of other departments are called in as well. In my time in the department this team has done excellent work, visited many centres in Canada and along the seaway. Marie, Whitby.
And Windsor?

speechtext:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There was great dissatisfaction there about two weeks ago when I was up.

speechtext:
I really do not understand why there should be dissatisfaction because we are moving right ahead with this program, and it is going to be very expensive. I believe it will meet the needs of the lakehead cities.
He asked also about the work being done in the lower St. Lawrence, and I have here the figures for that. There has been about $5 million spent there in the last four years on the different developments, such as Baie Comeau, Pointe au Pere and so on. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre referred largely to housing matters and I shall answer his questions later in the afternoon.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador advocated small works in small places. I agree with him that there is more

The department has tried to keep this thought always in mind, and we will have a look at the proposal that there should be more winches and small landing wharves. I wonder if the minister would permit me to ask one question at this time? speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The hon. member for Gloucester asked about three different projects, and I have reports here on all of them. In so far as the wharf at Maisonnette is concerned, the department has been considering various methods of improving harbour facilities for the fishermen at Maisonnette for some time now. However, its location has made our problem quite difficult in that the obvious manner of improving conditions would include dredging where the bottom is composed of rock. If 66968-9-279J
Supply-Public Works we could only find a harbour bottom composed of mud, it would be much simpler to get this work done.
Maisonnette is situated on the south shore of bay Chaleur between the two harbours of Blue Cove and Caraquet where good facilities are presently maintained. The department carried out improvements at Blue Cove last year and received tenders on June 3 for a large reconstruction project at Caraquet.
The existing facilities at Maisonnette constitute a high water landing only. Even a 200-foot extension to the outer end of the existing wharf would only provide 21 feet of water and this would be of little value. Any dredging along such an extension would be costly and involve considerable rock blasting, possibly endangering the structure. The minimum work which could be considered of real benefit would include dredging a 50-foot wide channel and a basin adjacent to the wharf. The estimated cost of this would be about $160,000 and in rough weather it would not afford very good protection for boats. The capital outlay required to provide improvements appears large when compared to the benefits to be derived. Nevertheless, I understand there has been a growth in the fishery in this area and the department is continuing its investigations as to the best method of improving the facilities. The federal Department of Fisheries is going to undertake a review of the economic conditions and future prospects. When the results of their study are known, we will be in a better position to assess the merit of the proposal for improved facilities at Maisonnette.
The problem at Maisonnette is not simple and does involve large capital outlays. I might refer to recent attempts by local fishermen to improve their lot. These fishermen got together and hired a bulldozer in order to cut a channel through the sandbar located close to the existing wharf so they could have more protection for their boats. However, I understand the sand movement caused the cut to fill in as quickly as it was bulldozed. These fishermen are to be highly commended for their initiative and efforts in this regard, and it is regrettable that these efforts were not more successful.
In so far as Tracadie is concerned, I may say a preliminary study of this project has been made. The results indicate that a much more comprehensive investigation will be required before the department will have sufficient information on which to base a decision. The assistance of the national research council has been sought and they have visited the location to determine what additional data is necessary for their work.

Supply-Public Works Either a mathematical analysis of conditions at the entrance to this harbour or a model study will be required. It may be necessary to request the Canadian hydrographic services people to carry out a complete sounding survey of the area.
The department maintains a wharf at Tracadie village, and I believe the fish landings at this structure have been maintained at a good level over recent years. Our problem at Tracadie concerns the entrance to this harbour, which is actually known as Tracadie gully and is only a channel running through two sand beaches. Years ago a considerable expenditure was made to protect this channel but, of late, indications are that nature is having its own way and the channel is being maintained without our help.
We are examining the need for: (a) removing the north breakwater; (b) constructing a causeway between the beach and Pointe Bouleau; and (c) the need for developing a deep draft harbour. The investigation to date indicates the cost of removing the ruins would not be commensurate with the benefits to be derived, and until the results of all studies are available no decision can be made on the other portions of the proposed work.

We had a survey made there by our interdepartmental team. The report they brought back was not only a good one but it was good reading. It was extremely interesting, particularly to one coming from the west coast where the conditions are completely different.
There are certain works on the Magdalen islands which are to be studied in conjunction with the national research council. They consist of Oyster pond, Portage du Cap and Etang des Caps.
As to Oyster pond, an amount of $500 was authorized on May 13 of this year for current survey work to be done by district officials. This is to obtain preparatory information for the further study by national research

council. The problem at this place is to effect an entrance into Oyster pond. The national research council are to study the effects of the littoral drift problem in order to determine what different possible entrances may be affected. If, in the preliminary investigation, it is indicated that construction would be warranted and a model study is indicated, this will be undertaken by the national research council.
With regard to Portage du Cap and Etang des Caps, the problem here is to arrange some means of getting the fishing craft from their hauled out position on the shore into the water. Again, this is a matter of studying the littoral drift to determine if any effective means of launching and withdrawing the boats from the water can be built, other than what would be required to build a structure extending out into deep water. Such a structure would be very long and would be of excessive cost. It is in an effort to build something within practical economic limits that the assistance of the national research council has been requested.
In addition to the above works, studies have been undertaken by district officials at Havre Aubert for the development of a protected harbour. An amount of $2,000 was authorized on May 4 of this year for this study which includes soundings and borings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister and the house would allow me one word before this item passes, because I am sure the house has given careful consideration to the administrative item concerning the minister's department. What prompts me to rise again are two matters. First, I think it was very fitting of the minister a moment ago to pay tribute to his officers upon his departure from his department. I think it is a nice gesture on the part of the minister who is about to sever connections with his department to refer to the close association which he has had with trusted officers in the department. I would like to add, if I may, a word to what the minister has said and to recall to the house the names of three of the officers who have been closely associated and connected with his department.
When I came to Ottawa, I am almost sorry to say 25 years ago-sorry because of the length of time-the then deputy minister of the Department of Public Works was James Hunter. He was, as the minister may recall, a very efficient and competent deputy minister. He held that office for many years. He was exceedingly sympathetic to representations made by members of parliament from all sides. He knew his department thoroughly. He took decisions with dispatch, and he was, I believe, all in all a very satisfactory and highly regarded public servant in the department. So much so was that the case that I believe that was one of the reasons why the building which now houses the Department of Public Works bears the name of the late James Hunter. I think I would have been remiss had I not risen to pay this tribute to him, not only because of my personal association with him over many, many years, but also because of the excellent reputation which is still associated with his name in the department.
After he left he was succeeded, I believe, by Mr. Emmett Murphy. As the house knows,

Supply-Public Works Mr. Emmett Murphy is now quite ill in a hospital in Ottawa. He is a graduate of Queen's University, an engineer of talent who had been associated with the work of the construction of the Welland canal and who, particularly during the war years, did a commendable job in the department of munitions and supply and 1 believe afterwards in the department of reconstruction. In his later years he became deputy minister of public works, and he did during the time that he was in office a very commendable job. The minister has referred to his own deputy minister, and I will not add to what he has already said.
The minister was also kind enough to pay a special tribute to his predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Winters, whose name has been mentioned on two or three occasions as being a minister of very high calibre, and we on this side of the house thank the minister for the reference which he made to the efficiency of his pre-iecessor, indeed a minister of great talent.
I would also like to refer to another minister with whom I sat in the house for many years and who, like the Minister of Public Works now, held the position of house leader for a long time. That was the Hon. Alphonse Fournier, the former member for Hull, who is now a member of the Exchequer Court of Canada. While I was not in the ministry when he was sworn in-I came in later-I know of the tremendous amount of work and painstaking care which he gave to the duties that were entrusted to him, and I felt that on this occasion the minister would not mind if at this stage I said a word about his devotion to duty.
Now may I just take another few minutes and I will resume my seat. I would like to tell the minister that I think on the whole he is adopting the right attitude in so far as port development and port facilities are concerned. But what I have great fear of is this. I do not think there is the over-all planning that there should be. It seems to me that when the planning is entrusted to two and three departments there is bound to be some confusion. In the first place, I think there should be-I do not want to repeat what I said earlier-an economic survey of the whole area from the lower St. Lawrence right up to the head of the lakes. I also think that the minister or his successor should entrust the house with the plans that the department has for the development of these ports. It is a nice thing to be able to say that $5 million is spent here, $8 million spent here, and $10 million spent there. That looks good, but having regard to the movement of the traffic, I do not think anybody quite knows just how the traffic is going to move. I realize it is not an easy job and

that is why it seems to me that there must be a planning of works in these ports in conjunction with an economic survey. Where is the traffic going to move? What kind of traffic will it be? The plan that the minister has should jibe with that which the Minister of Transport has or the national harbours board; otherwise there is bound to be confusion.
Let me remind the minister of what he used to tell me when I took up my estimates in the Department of Transport concerning the national harbours board and the port of Vancouver. I remember I used to come down with the estimates concerning Vancouver and cite large amounts. The minister was grateful for the amounts which went for port development and port facilities in the city of Vancouver, but repeatedly he would come back and say, "I want to know what the plans are for the future in the city of Vancouver", and he had every right to demand them. We on this side of the house will not insist unduly about that, but I wonder whether the minister would be good enough to bring this to the attention of the gentleman who will succeed him, because this is a matter which cannot be done over a period of months. It is a matter which must take time. All of us are interested in this problem, and I am sure no one is interested more than he and his officers. Everyone must realize that there has to be an over-all plan and that that plan must fit in with those of the various departments. I just give that in conclusion as another thought which I trust the minister will give attention to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would like to join in the tribute that the hon. member has paid to the other Canadians who have taken such a great part in the work of the department. The hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Royal, the hon. member for Laurier, and I are the only members of the class which came here in 1935. I hope that as Minister of Public Works he will give me ready co-operation in a matter about which I now intend to say a few words. The minister spoke earlier in the day about the satisfaction he derived from smaller works in smaller places. It is about one of those works that I wish to say something. I have here a long petition which comes from a group of my constituents who live in the township of Rochester near the village of St. Joachim, Ontario, in the riding which I have the honour to represent in this house. The petition has to do with the river Ruscomb and its outlet at lake St. Clair. This is a matter which was looked into in the middle of February by the department at my request. The petition has to do with properties which are located on the Ruscomb river approaching the mouth of lake St. Clair, including Rochester beach, what is known as the Renaud subdivision, the Tellier subdivision and certain other areas along both sides of the river Ruscomb.
There has to be some deepening of this river and some work at the mouth touching lake St. Clair. This is not a matter which will involve much expenditure, but as an indication of the constructive way in which my constituents have approached this matter, may I say that they have put forward the idea that this might be a joint operation in which the province of Ontario could participate. They hope that the river Ruscomb outlet may be cleaned and deepened, thereby saving the banks and generally providing a satisfactory approach to historic lake St. Clair.
I would be very grateful if the minister could give this matter his consideration, and I hope this will be one of the hon. gentleman's final acts as Minister of Public Works. Other hon. members have suggested that he should recommend strongly to his successor that this or that action be taken. I would ask him, on the merits of this particular case, to make a favourable decision himself and
Supply-Public Works give my constituents the opportunity of remembering that as a result of the intervention of their member they received from the man who was minister of public works, now Canada's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, the rectification of this situation in a way which I believe the situation warrants.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On Saturday, October 25, 1958, at about 8.20 a.m., an explosion occurred in premises located at 246-48 Slater Street. It is alleged to have resulted from the ignition of natural gas which had escaped into that building. The crown-owned Jackson building, situated directly across the street from the explosion, suffered great damage. The structural frame was unharmed but practically all windows and doors, practically all interior partitions and the majority of the lighting fixtures and building fittings received maximum damage. The contents were also severely blown about. Fortunately, there was no loss of life or severe injury in the building. If the blast had not occurred on a Saturday morning there might have been hundreds of people killed or seriously injured.
The damage was such that the building was uninhabitable. The three departments who occupied the building were housed elsewhere; the income tax branch in the trade and commerce building, the headquarters of the Department of National Health and Welfare in the Copeland building and the civil service commission in No. 1 temporary building. To bring the building back into use as quickly as possible, the remedial work was divided into four phases to allow planning for the occupants to go forward while repairs to the fabric to the building were being effected.
Phases 1 and 2 have been completed. In these contracts the exterior and interior fabric of the building was renewed and space on the lower three floors was prepared for the income tax branch. They occupied the building during the last week of March.
Phases 3 and 4 will complete the renovation of the building and the building services, and the preparation of the upper floors for the use of the civil service commission and the Department of National Health and Welfare. These latter two departments are scheduled to reoccupy the building in October.
An information has been filed in the Exchequer Court of Canada, naming as defendants the Consumers' Gas Company, who distribute natural gas in Ottawa; Addresso-graph-Multigraph of Canada, Limited, who were tenants in the building where the explosion occurred; and the Lumor Interests Limited, who were owners of the same building. We are claiming from them damages in the amount of $1,220,820, as well as the costs of the action and such further and other relief as the court may deem meet.

I might say that the property and building management branch of the department did a wonderful job at the time of the accident. They did a splendid job in quickly housing these different governmental branches. The explosion occurred on Saturday and provision for temporary accommodation was made for Monday morning. It was an outstanding piece of work.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The second question is, can the minister tell us, very briefly, what progress is being made in harbour development at St. John's?

I omitted to mention on the general item, Mr. Chairman, the fact that it has been decided to locate community stages in the easterly part of St. John's harbour known as the battery. This decision was reached because of the importance of this area as a fishing centre. It is not generally realized that there are over 200 fishermen actively engaged in fishing out of St. John's, and who contribute a great deal to the economy of the city of St. John's. The majority of these fishermen are located in that part of the harbour known as the battery.
My point is that they have no facilities there, and there have not been any facilities for fishermen at that location down through the years. In view of this fact the Department of Fisheries, and the Department of Public Works, in their wisdom, decided to locate community stages there. This part of St. John's harbour is not part of the city of St. John's and is not serviced by the municipality. I wonder, therefore, if the minister and his officials would give consideration to conducting a survey to ascertain what facilities might be provided in addition to the community stages to facilitate the fishery in this important part of St. John's. I am thinking of such facilities as a fisherman's wharf, some sort of breakwater to protect the boats and the gear of the fishermen.
The other point I should like to make now, Mr. Chairman, is that in view of the work that is currently being undertaken at Bell island with respect to the extension of the wharf and the erection and construction of a new warehouse, and bearing in mind the fact that a new ferryboat is now under construction to service Bell island, would the minister and his officials take into consideration for next year's estimates the provision of a breakwater at Bell island which would provide a basin for shipping and provide artificial harbour facilities? My personal knowledge of this area indicates that this is the only place along the Northumberland strait which is not provided with the necessary facilities for fishing. Mr. Chairman, for the last two hours I have not heard anyone congratulating the Minister of Public Works on his appointment to the external affairs portfolio. After throwing bouquets at the minister, I may have a few criticisms to bring before the committee in relation to some matters which may be of no importance to many constituencies but which are of great importance to my constituency of Chambly-Rouville.
First I want to thank the minister for the attention with which he has favoured my constituency. I thank him for the laige amount provided for the constituency of Chambly-Rouville on the Richelieu river for retaining walls. The minister did not have the reputation of handing out too much money on this item but, whether I am lucky or not, I think Chambly-Rouville will get its fair share this year.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I want to emphasize the case of the city of Beloeil, one of the finest municipalities in the province of Quebec, where retaining walls had already been erected in various places in front of this or that owner's lot or in front of another property located a little further. They used to build retaining walls to please certain people who reciprocated the same favour to the member around election time.
Since the Conservative government was elected, this policy was somewhat abandoned. The intention was to be fair towards everybody, although in other ridings they are in the same situation. This government is being charged with favouring supporters of the Liberal party while failing to do the same thing for supporters of the Conservative party.
I should like to put this on the record of the house so that it be known that we favour that policy because it is fair to everyone. The completion of the retaining walls, partially built by the Liberals, is an illustration of what the Conservative party is now doing to repair the mistakes made by the previous government and to fulfil the promises made by the members, particularly those who represented the constituency of Chambly-Rouville.
A moment ago, I heard an hon. member attempting to claim for himself the credit which is due to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) for carrying out a program in.

his constituency. He said that the work had been carried out at the time of the Liberal party. Perhaps the program had been started by the Liberal party, but it was carried to completion under the Conservative regime. I am surprised to hear people say we are piling deficits upon deficits, but if we are doing so, it is to finish the work begun by the Liberals.
Mr. Chairman, let us now say a word about the retaining wall in Beloeil; it was an old dream of the former secretary of state, Mr. Roch Pinard. I imagine that the former Liberal member of the legislative assembly, the present mayor of Beloeil, will soon write a letter to the minister somewhat similar to the one which the minister read into the record earlier this afternoon.

In Chambly, at the mouth of Chambly canal, there is some erosion caused by navigation.
I am not the only one to believe that, on the basis of reports from the department or from certain officials of the department, stating that very little erosion was being caused by navigation, the department refuses to build a retaining wall. I do not agree with them and I ask the minister to give instructions to his department to make a further study of the matter. It might be convenient to make it a practice of consulting the member who, when something is not done right, receives the representations and the criticisms of all the voters, but seldom receives congratulations from his opponents. When there is something wrong, the practice should be to consult the people's representative and to ask his opinion, particularly about retaining walls and especially when it is a matter of building such walls.
I do not know who has been consulted about that retaining wall, but I do know that the matter should be studied. I know that a letter will be sent to the minister by the city council of Chambly, since the erosion is due in part, at least, to navigation, a situation which seems inevitable at the mouth of the Chambly canal. I wonder if it is recognized in the department that erosion is partly due to navigation. I wonder if it would not be necessary to build there, either this year or next, the retaining wall already begun in 1932 by the Conservative party, over a length of about 1,000 feet, continued by the Liberal party over a length of about 100 feet, and which should be continued by this government over the rest of the required length.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Steep Rock is a community of about 300 people located on the east shore of lake Manitoba, 140 miles by

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. The project was estimated at $70,000. I have now a better explanation for the wharf at Steep Rock.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I laid a good foundation, but here is the whole story. This amount of $16,000 is required for the construction of an extension to the wharf to provide additional berthing and landing facilities. The existing structure is not long enough to accommodate the barges and other craft using it, since only the inner side, with 85


feet of berthing space, can be used. There are no other public wharves on lake Manitoba.
The wharf is used by cattle ranchers on Peonan point, four miles west of Steep Rock, who transport cattle and supplies by barge to and from Steep Rock, the nearest road and rail link. Their only alternative is to go by road around the north end of lake Manitoba to St. Martin on the C.N.R. This is a journey of 35 to 40 miles and the road becomes impassable in wet weather. For these reasons, the route is no longer used. The ranchers on Peonan point are the only ranchers who transport their cattle by barge to a shipping point. Other ranchers on both sides of lake Manitoba are close to a highway or railway, so that there is no advantage in crossing the lake.
The wharf is also used by small private and tourist boats and a few aircraft. Fishermen ship supplies over the wharf in the late fall of the year. Total craft using the wharf are two barges, three boats-over 30 feet-with inboard engines and 50 smaller outboard powered boats. The value of produce, supplies and equipment shipped over the wharf each year is estimated as follows: cattle, $80,000; fuel and gas, $4,000; machinery, $20,000; food, etc. $4,000; fishing equipment, $12,000. The two cattle barges are 54 feet and 60 feet long, respectively. An average of two trips per week are made by the barges between June and freeze-up. Approximately 1,800 head of cattle are at present on Peonan point and this number is expected to increase.
