I must preface my brief remarks on this item by drawing to the minister's attention the expanding economy of the Kootenay district and its continuous growth and every evidence of very large expansion of the forest industry, in the future. We have at the present time the operations of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company which are also expanding, and we have a very large development of the forest industry.
During last year 300 million feet of lumber were sawn inside the Nelson forest district, a good indication of what is to come, and at the present time construction has started on the foundations of a $50 million pulp mill at Castlegar. So it is not a question of providing services or buildings in a declining economy or in a country where there will be ghost towns. The minister knows that well enough.
I want to bring to his attention the changing pattern in navigation on the lakes. As the minister knows, up to a few years ago we had sternwheel steamers on passenger service and large steam tugs working for the lumber companies, hauling railroad barges or barges carrying iron ore for mining companies. The sternwheel steamers have ceased to operate and the pattern of navigation now is a larger number of small diesel tugs-they are not required to be as large in order to be as powerful-plus a great increase in the use of the lakes by small pleasure craft. Last year about 100 small craft came up the Columbia river, some from as far as Portland at the mouth of the Columbia being portaged around the dams in the United States by low-boys. I was told by some of these visitors from the United States that the increase in this traffic this year will be quite considerable, with every expectation of a rapid increase as the years go by to tourist camp operators. To indicate what that means, there were 22 of these small craft from the United States which arrived on the Saturday preceding Labour Day at St. Leon and Hot Springs and before they left they left $1,200 in cash. That was only 22 out of 80 that came up the river from the United States on Labour Day. Some went to Revelstoke, others
Supply-Public Works came down the Kootenay river and were launched at various places on the Kootenay lake. The visits of these small craft are of great importance to the district and a great help to tourist resort operators who, as the minister knows, have to skim their cream in about four months of the year. I mention this to illustrate the stability of the economy and the changing pattern of navigation which, I think, was not fully understood by some of the minister's district officials a year or so ago.
It is a strange thing, but in the Kootenays we get overlooked on so many occasions. We had few visits from cabinet ministers of the Liberal government during the years it was in office. We have had a few more since the present government came to power by the Minister of Public Works but purely on account of the fact that his home town is in my constituency, and we are most fortunate in that respect. However, I think that with the lure of larger works on the coast district engineers are inclined to fail to realize to the fullest extent the importance of the federal Department of Public Works to our district.
I must say that the people in Boswell are delighted with the launching way that has been built there, and I am informed a considerable number of United States craft have already this year been launched there. The same applies to the people of Kaslo and the people of Burton who are very pleased that reconsideration was given to the demolition of the Burton wharf and to its reconstruction and improvement as a wharf and launching way.
I suggest to the minister that very serious consideration should be given before the demolition of any wharf is undertaken. I was sorry a few years ago that the Halcyon wharf was demolished. I was inspector of that wharf when it was built. The piling was sound; only a few planks needed replacing. The hotel Halcyon had burned down, so there was apparently no use for the wharf. However, that wharf was the only wharf between Arrowhead and Nakusp at which tugs could tie up in the event of a storm. A number of skippers have told me they wish the wharf was still there to tie up to.
I urge that consideration be given to the new needs for a wharf before there is any further demolition undertaken.
There is a great increase in the ownership of small water craft in the Rossland-Trail district. The residents of that district would like to see a launching way at a site below Trail the name of which I forget at this moment. It is a suitable site. If this work cannot be undertaken this year

Supply-Public Works
I urge consideration of its construction next year. There will be a large use for a launching way near Trail.
The chamber of commerce of the village of New Denver is anxious to have a launching way built there at an excellent site. The minister knows all about it. I hope it will be included in plans for next year with respect to the navigation welfare of Kootenay West.
I must say how pleased the people of the district are that the department decided to build a new wharf at Galena bay. There will soon be a great deal of traffic at that point. The traffic is increasing every year. Possibly the minister does not know that it is likely that the road between Nakusp and Galena bay to the very wharf in question will be completed this year. It is partially completed now. Three or four days ago my son-in-law informed me that another construction crew is expected to start working soon on the portion between St. Leon and Galena bay. It is fortunate that the department has decided to rebuild this wharf because it will be at the apex of two routes of traffic going north, one from the Kootenay lake the other from Nakusp. We were very pleased that the department decided to make provision for the construction of that important wharf in the estimates this year.
Now I have a few suggestions to make before I sit down. I suggest that everything be done to keep the permanent staff employed rather than bringing in other persons. The dredge has a crew of experienced men. A number of these men have worked on the Arrow lakes for many years. At certain times they are laid off and the dredge employed on day work for the department. I suggest that in the type of construction that has to be undertaken with launching ways and wharves on Arrow, Kootenay, Slocan, and other lakes day labour is cheaper than contract work. That was demonstrated when the Nakusp wharf was built. I was informed by the officials that they saved several thousand dollars with day labour. An outside contractor has to make allowance for bringing in equipment and other costs. These men are experienced and know what to do. When you employ these men you are employing men who have had experience with running pile drivers, building wharves and works of that type. I suggest that every effort be made to keep the permanent crew on the dredge employed for as great a part of the year as possible in this way.
I mentioned that every consideration should be given to the maintenance of the present wharves as long as they can be repaired at any reasonable cost.
[Mr. Herridge.l
I was in Trout lake recently. There is a small wharf at the north end. It is an isolated spot with only seven permanent residents. Didn't I enjoy, what shall I say, the evidence of the democratic spirit that exists there. I was told an oil man came in and bought the hotel and spent about $40,000 on it and put in a cocktail lounge. He told the old trappers and prospectors, one of whom was in our battalion, "I do not want you old birds around here. I intend to attract high class clients." They had a vote on the question and all voted against the cocktail lounge. He lost out by failing to give consideration to the old time pioneer residents of whom I am very fond.
I suggest that wharf be kept in repair, as it is used as a launching way in the summer. It is a good sound wharf. There is a necessity for a similar small structure at the south end of Trout lake near Argenta. Tourists drive up from the south and fish in Trout lake and then pull up their boats at the north end.
The members of the Nakusp launch club of which I am a member brought to my attention the fact that they were interested to note that a breakwater had been built at Okanagan Landing last year. They wanted me to put in a plug for them. I do not suggest that this could be done overnight but if there is any more money available for this purpose I urge the minister and the deputy minister to give consideration to this. Money would be well spent on such a breakwater.
I now mention the question of dredging and pay particular tribute to a man employed by the department who knows dredging. He has had experience in the Royal Navy and as captain of a dredge. He has worked on wharves and river improvements for many years. This gentleman is in charge of floating equipment in the office in Vancouver. If the minister or the deputy minister have any questions about floating equipment in the interior of British Columbia I suggest that they take the advice of this gentleman. He is a practical person with experience.
I now bring to the minister's attention a problem arising out of the great increase in the lumber industry in the Kootenays. Millions of additional feet are being sawn every year. Millions of feet of logs are being towed from the north arm of the Arrow lake down to the mills at Nakusp. At the present time there is a narrow channel dredged toward Arrowhead for various craft to approach the wharf. It is quite wide enough for that purpose but not wide enough for tugs towing logs. It is possible for a tug to come out towing one million feet at high water but from medium water on it is very difficult. The tug cannot proceed west far enough to turn the boom into the channel without touching bottom. In extremely low water the channel is not wide

enough to allow the logs to go through. One million feet of logs were tied up for several days on two occasions last year. The captain could not swing the boom in question. Sometimes if they cannot go far enough west to make the turn the wind will blow the boom to the shallows on the east side of the cut. I know there are about ten million feet of logs coming out of the north arm this year.
There is a new sawmill being build at Arrowhead and another at Nakusp. It is expected all the mills there will require fifty million feet of logs this year. I am not blaming the department for the situation because these developments are happening, as it were, overnight. I suggest that a survey be made of the situation with respect to the dredging of the mouth of the Columbia toward the present Arrowhead dock to see if the cut could not be widened to some extent, and possibly some of the easterly bar taken off so tugs towing booms would not have difficulty making the turn.
At the present time the channel is far too narrow. I have been asked by those interested in the lumber industry and particularly the men towing logs to bring this to the minister's attention. I am quite sure that if the minister's officials went into the district they could get a very good description of the difficulties that occur at the present time from the captains of the tugs and other craft.
This concludes my suggestions, Mr. Chairman. The minister knows that I never ask for anything that is not absolutely essential.

Before the minister replies to the hon. member, knowing his enthusiasm for the interior of British Columbia, I am hoping he is not going to start building wharves for seven people on the lakes of British Columbia when there are 700 in many places on the Atlantic coast who still need wharves.

I must in my first remarks thank the minister for his splendid construction of a breakwater at Gibsons, British Columbia, thereby showing the good wisdom he has displayed in constructing this facility. The main matter which I wish to bring up at this time is the matter of policy. I think it should be brought to the attention of the committee. I am sure the minister is fully conversant with this matter and will discuss it with his successor. It has to do with the increasing need for protective facilities for the thousands of small boat owners and operators who are plying the British Columbia coastal waters in increasing numbers as the weeks go by. In the past summer it was estimated that on weekends on the lower mainland area of the coastal waters somewhere in the neighbourhood of 14,000 to 15,000 craft were at sea. At the present time no policy exists within the structure of the federal government or the provincial government to provide shelter. This means that in the event of a sudden blow some weekend there would be no safety shelter available and without such shelter we can, I am sure, look forward in the future in our west coast waters to one of the world's great maritime tragedies. What the answer is I am sure I do not know; but I would submit that this matter is deserving of immediate and early study. Possibly it should be approached from the point of view of assessing a proper licence fee to those who are operating this type of craft in order that this shelter may be provided. Development Engineering Services, Highways Division, Contribution Towards Construction of Dam over Tantramar River, N.B.-$84,375 (New Item)
This amount is required to cover a contribution by the Department of Public Works to the province of New Brunswick, in respect of the construction of a dam over the Tantramar river, which will form a part of the trans-Canada highway. This work is being done by the maritime marshland rehabilitation administration under an agreement with the province of New Brunswick. This structure is to serve the dual purpose of a marshland protection work, as well as a section of the trans-Canada highway.
Supply-Public Works
Order in council P.C. 1957/684 dated 9 May, 1957, authorized the construction of the Tantramar river dam under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and granted to the Minister of Agriculture authority to execute with the province of New Brunswick an agreement for the construction of the dam, which was to include provision for a highway crossing. The basis of sharing in the cost was that the federal government (Department of Agriculture) would undertake 77.5% of the cost and the province of New Brunswick ihe remaining 22.5%. In addition, the arrangement was that half of the payments made by the province to the maritime marshland rehabilitation administration were to be paid by the federal Department of Public Works (Highways Division).
The above arrangement is altogether similar in principle to one which was made with the province of Nova Scotia in the fiscal year 1955-56, with respect to a contribution towards the construction of a dam at the Ingonish river. At that time the deputy attorney general, Department of Justice, advised that he was unable to find authority under the trans-Canada highway agreement for a contribution by Canada to the province and advised that if it was decided to proceed with the joint project that the best method would be to enter an appropriate item in the estimates. In view of the fact that the cost of the dam was increased in order to make provision for a roadway crossing for the trans-Canada highway, it was considered that the item should be included in the public works estimates.
The contract for the Tantramar dam has now been awarded to the Modern Construction Company at a cost of $528,010. In addition to this amount, it is estimated that other items will bring the total to $750,000. Under the above mentioned order in council, New Brunswick's share of this amount is 224% or $168,750. The share of the federal Department of Public Works is, therefore $84,375. This amount would be subject to downward revision if, when all accounts are in for the project, the total expenditure is less than $750,000.
